title: Cardiovascular and Respiratory Medicine
topics: Cardiovascular and respiratory structure and function
Causes and risk factors of common diseases
Basic clinical skills and function tests
Drug treatment of heart and lung disease

notes.h: Cardiorespiratory physiology: pump, vessels, lungs and gas transport
notes.body:
The heart
- Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume, about 5 L/min at rest. Stroke volume depends on preload (Frank-Starling: more stretch gives a stronger contraction), afterload and contractility.
- MAP ≈ diastolic + ⅓ pulse pressure, and physiologically MAP = cardiac output × total peripheral resistance.
- Poiseuille: resistance = 8ηL ÷ πr⁴, so halving arteriolar radius raises resistance 16-fold.
- SA node: slow depolarisation from the funny current (If, via HCN channels) then T-type Ca²⁺; the upstroke is L-type Ca²⁺, not fast Na⁺. Ventricular myocytes have phase 0 Na⁺ influx, a phase 2 Ca²⁺ plateau, and a long refractory period, so they cannot be tetanised.
- Excitation-contraction coupling: Ca²⁺ entry triggers calcium-induced calcium release via RyR2; relaxation needs SERCA and the Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger.
- The AV node delays conduction (about 0.1 s) and filters fast atrial rates.
- Baroreflex: carotid sinus (IX) and aortic arch (X) afferents go to the nucleus tractus solitarius. Falling pressure increases sympathetic and reduces vagal outflow.
- Left ventricular coronary flow occurs mainly in diastole, so tachycardia reduces supply while raising demand.
- Starling forces: hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out, oncotic pressure (albumin) pulls it in, and lymph clears the excess. Low albumin causes oedema.

The lungs
- Type I pneumocytes carry out gas exchange; type II secrete surfactant and regenerate the epithelium. Surfactant lowers surface tension, stabilising small alveoli (Laplace, P = 2T/r) and raising compliance.
- Compliance (ΔV/ΔP) falls in fibrosis and rises in emphysema. FRC is where lung recoil balances chest wall recoil.
- Alveolar ventilation = (tidal volume − dead space) × rate. Fick's law: diffusion ∝ area × gradient ÷ thickness.
- V/Q is high at the apex and low at the base. Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction diverts blood from poorly ventilated alveoli.
- The O₂–Hb curve is sigmoid because of cooperative binding. It shifts right with raised CO₂ and H⁺ (the Bohr effect), temperature and 2,3-BPG. Most CO₂ travels as bicarbonate; the Haldane effect means deoxygenated Hb carries more CO₂.
- Central chemoreceptors sense CSF H⁺ from CO₂ and provide most resting drive. Peripheral (carotid and aortic) receptors respond strongly once PaO₂ falls below about 8 kPa.

Worked examples
- Fick: VO₂ 300 mL/min, CaO₂ 200 mL/L, CvO₂ 150 mL/L gives cardiac output = 300 ÷ 50 = 6 L/min. If output falls with VO₂ unchanged, extraction rises and CvO₂ falls.
- Tidal volume 500 mL at 12/min with 150 mL dead space gives 4.2 L/min alveolar ventilation; 250 mL at 24/min gives only 2.4 L/min.

Exam pitfalls
- Attributing the SA node upstroke to Na⁺.
- Saying the lung apex is better perfused.
- Forgetting that pulmonary vessels constrict, not dilate, in hypoxia.

notes.h: Causes and risk factors of common cardiorespiratory disease
notes.body:
Atherosclerosis
Endothelial dysfunction lets LDL enter the intima, where it is oxidised. Macrophages take it up to form foam cells (fatty streak), and smooth muscle cells lay down a fibrous cap over a lipid core. Vulnerable plaques have thin caps, large necrotic cores and many macrophages. Rupture or erosion causes thrombosis and acute coronary syndrome. Stable angina reflects a fixed narrowing that limits flow only when demand rises.

Risk factors
- Modifiable: smoking, hypertension, raised LDL or non-HDL cholesterol, diabetes, obesity, inactivity, diet and alcohol. Non-modifiable: age, male sex, family history of premature disease and ethnicity.
- QRISK3 estimates 10-year cardiovascular risk. NICE uses 10% or more as the usual threshold for offering a statin in primary prevention.
- Pack-years = (cigarettes per day ÷ 20) × years smoked.
- Familial hypercholesterolaemia is usually autosomal dominant (LDL receptor, APOB or PCSK9 variants). It causes very high LDL, tendon xanthomata and premature coronary disease, so test first-degree relatives.
- Most hypertension is essential. Secondary causes include renal disease, renal artery stenosis, hyperaldosteronism, phaeochromocytoma, Cushing's and coarctation.

Thrombosis and heart disease
- Virchow's triad: stasis, hypercoagulability and vessel wall injury. VTE risks include surgery, immobility, cancer, pregnancy, oestrogens, previous VTE and thrombophilia.
- AF causes stasis in the left atrial appendage, leading to thrombus and stroke.
- Heart failure is commonly due to coronary disease and hypertension. HFrEF is EF 40% or less; HFpEF is 50% or more; 41–49% is mildly reduced.
- Rheumatic heart disease follows group A streptococcal infection through molecular mimicry; mitral stenosis is the classic chronic lesion. In endocarditis, Staphylococcus aureus is now the commonest organism.

Lung disease
- COPD is mainly caused by smoking. The protease–antiprotease imbalance destroys alveolar walls. Centriacinar, upper-lobe emphysema is typical of smoking; panacinar, lower-lobe emphysema of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. Chronic bronchitis means productive cough for 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years.
- Allergic asthma involves IgE-sensitised mast cells and Th2 cytokines (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13). Triggers include viruses, allergens, cold, exercise and β-blockers.
- Cystic fibrosis is autosomal recessive, caused by CFTR variants (commonly F508del). Streptococcus pneumoniae is the commonest cause of community-acquired pneumonia.
- Lung cancer is caused mainly by smoking, with radon and asbestos also important. Asbestos also causes plaques, asbestosis and mesothelioma. Hypoxic lung disease leads to cor pulmonale. AAA screening is offered to men in the year they turn 65.

Worked example: 20 cigarettes a day from age 17 to 62 is (20 ÷ 20) × 45 = 45 pack-years.

Exam pitfalls
- Assuming the tightest stenosis is the one that ruptures.
- Linking panacinar emphysema to smoking rather than alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

ECG
- At 25 mm/s, a small square is 0.04 s and a large square 0.2 s. For a regular rhythm, rate = 300 ÷ large squares between R waves; for an irregular one, count QRS complexes in 10 s and multiply by 6.
- Normal: PR 0.12–0.20 s, QRS under 0.12 s.
- Territories: inferior leads (II, III, aVF) usually the RCA; V1–V4 the LAD; lateral leads (I, aVL, V5–V6) the circumflex.
- STEMI: new J-point ST elevation in two contiguous leads. AF shows an irregularly irregular rhythm with no P waves. Hyperkalaemia gives peaked T waves, then loss of P waves, a broad QRS and a sine wave.

Lung function and gases
- Obstruction is FEV1/FVC below 0.7 (or the lower limit of normal). Restriction is low FVC with a normal or high ratio. A rise in FEV1 of at least 12% and 200 mL after bronchodilator suggests asthma.
- TLCO falls in emphysema, interstitial disease, pulmonary vascular disease and anaemia.
- ABG normal values: pH 7.35–7.45, PaO₂ about 10–13 kPa, PaCO₂ 4.7–6.0 kPa, HCO₃⁻ 22–26 mmol/L. Type 1 failure is PaO₂ below 8 kPa with normal or low PaCO₂; type 2 adds PaCO₂ above about 6 kPa.
- ABG order: oxygenation (with FiO₂), pH, PaCO₂, HCO₃⁻, then compensation.
- PAO₂ ≈ 20 − PaCO₂/0.8 kPa on air at sea level. A raised A–a gradient indicates V/Q mismatch, shunt or a diffusion problem.

Examination
- S1 is mitral and tricuspid closure; S2 is aortic and pulmonary closure, splitting on inspiration. Murmurs: aortic stenosis, ejection systolic to the carotids; mitral regurgitation, pansystolic to the axilla; aortic regurgitation, early diastolic; mitral stenosis, mid-diastolic rumble.
- JVP is normally up to about 3–4 cm above the sternal angle at 45°.
- Percussion: dull in consolidation, stony dull in effusion, hyper-resonant in pneumothorax. The trachea is pushed away by tension or massive effusion and pulled towards collapse or fibrosis.
- COPD alone does not cause clubbing.

Other tests
- Troponin rises and/or falls in MI but is also raised in PE, sepsis, heart failure and renal failure.
- A normal BNP or NT-proBNP makes heart failure unlikely. D-dimer is sensitive but non-specific.
- Pulse oximetry misses hypercapnia, misleads in CO poisoning and may overestimate saturation in darker skin.
- NICE diagnoses hypertension by ambulatory (or home) monitoring after a clinic reading of 140/90 mmHg or above.

Worked example: PaCO₂ 3.6 kPa and PaO₂ 9.0 kPa on air give PAO₂ ≈ 20 − 4.5 = 15.5 kPa, so the A–a gradient is 6.5 kPa, markedly raised for a 30-year-old. Consider PE.

Exam pitfalls
- Reading a normal PaO₂ as reassuring without knowing the FiO₂.

No doses are given here; see the BNF.

Hypertension and angina
- ACE inhibitors block angiotensin II formation and bradykinin breakdown, which causes the dry cough. Other risks are angioedema, hyperkalaemia and renal impairment, and they are avoided in pregnancy. ARBs block AT1 receptors with less cough.
- Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers dilate arterioles and cause ankle oedema that diuretics do not relieve. Verapamil and diltiazem slow the nodes; verapamil must not be combined with β-blockers (diltiazem only cautiously).
- Thiazide-like diuretics act on the distal tubule Na⁺/Cl⁻ cotransporter; loop diuretics act on NKCC2. Both cause hypokalaemia.
- NICE generally offers an ACE inhibitor or ARB first for adults under 55 or with type 2 diabetes, and a calcium channel blocker for those 55 or over, or of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin at any age, without diabetes.
- β-blockers lower rate, contractility and oxygen demand. GTN donates nitric oxide, raising cGMP and causing venodilation that lowers preload; it must never be combined with PDE5 inhibitors.

Thrombosis and lipids
- Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, which upregulates hepatic LDL receptors.
- Aspirin irreversibly acetylates platelet COX-1, blocking thromboxane A₂ for the platelet's lifespan. P2Y12 inhibitors (clopidogrel, prasugrel, ticagrelor) are added for dual antiplatelet therapy after ACS, given for a limited time to balance bleeding risk.
- Warfarin blocks vitamin K epoxide reductase and is monitored by INR. DOACs inhibit factor Xa or thrombin (dabigatran).

Heart failure (HFrEF)
Loop diuretics relieve congestion but do not improve survival. ACE inhibitors or ARBs (or sacubitril/valsartan, never with an ACE inhibitor), β-blockers such as bisoprolol, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists and SGLT2 inhibitors block maladaptive neurohormonal activation and improve outcomes. Digoxin inhibits Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and raises vagal tone. Its toxicity is worsened by hypokalaemia, renal impairment and amiodarone.

Arrhythmias
Vaughan Williams classes: I Na⁺ block, II β-blockers, III K⁺ block (amiodarone, which can affect the thyroid, lungs and liver), IV rate-limiting CCBs. Adenosine causes transient AV block to end re-entrant SVT and is avoided in asthma.

Airways
- Salbutamol (β2 agonist) raises cAMP and can cause tremor, tachycardia and hypokalaemia. Inhaled corticosteroids suppress inflammatory gene transcription; rinsing reduces candidiasis. LAMAs block M3 receptors.
- Montelukast blocks CysLT1 and carries neuropsychiatric warnings. Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic index.
- The 2024 BTS/NICE/SIGN asthma guideline offers new adult and adolescent patients as-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol (AIR) rather than a SABA alone.
- Oxygen targets are 94–98% for most patients, or 88–92% if at risk of hypercapnia.

Worked example: a man on digoxin starts high-dose furosemide and develops nausea, confusion and ectopics. Hypokalaemia increases digoxin binding to Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, causing toxicity.

Exam pitfalls
- Giving a β-blocker with verapamil.
- Expecting loop diuretics to improve HFrEF survival.

notes.h: Clinical decision-making: probability, scores and bias
notes.body:
Diagnostic tests
- Sensitivity = TP ÷ (TP + FN): a sensitive negative rules out (SnNout). Specificity = TN ÷ (TN + FP): a specific positive rules in (SpPin).
- PPV = TP ÷ (TP + FP) and NPV = TN ÷ (TN + FN). Both depend on prevalence.
- LR+ = sensitivity ÷ (1 − specificity); LR− = (1 − sensitivity) ÷ specificity. Post-test odds = pre-test odds × LR.
- Spectrum bias: accuracy in clear-cut cases overstates real-world performance.
- Treatment effects: ARR = control rate − treated rate; RRR = ARR ÷ control rate; NNT = 1 ÷ ARR.

Assessment and scores
- ABCDE: assess and treat in order, reassess after each intervention and call for help early.
- NEWS2: an aggregate of 5 or more triggers urgent review, 7 or more an emergency response, and a 3 in any single parameter urgent review.
- CURB-65 (confusion, urea over 7, RR 30 or more, low BP, age 65 or over) estimates pneumonia mortality and guides place of care.
- Wells (two-level, NICE): over 4 means PE is likely, so go to CTPA; 4 or less means do a D-dimer first.
- CHA₂DS₂-VASc estimates stroke risk in AF. NICE offers anticoagulation at 2 or more and considers it for men at 1. ORBIT assesses bleeding risk to address modifiable factors, not to withhold anticoagulation by itself. European guidance (2024) drops the sex criterion; follow local guidance.
- Life-threatening chest pain causes to exclude: ACS, aortic dissection, PE, tension pneumothorax, tamponade and oesophageal rupture.

Reasoning and communication
- Dual-process theory: fast pattern recognition (System 1) checked by analytical reasoning (System 2).
- Anchoring and premature closure are countered by asking 'what else could this be?' and using structured differentials.
- SBAR structures escalation. Shared decision-making combines evidence with patient values, as expected after Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board (2015).

Worked examples
- D-dimer with sensitivity 95% and specificity 50% in 1,000 patients at 10% prevalence: TP 95, FN 5, TN 450, FP 450. PPV = 95/545 ≈ 17% and NPV = 450/455 ≈ 99%. At 40% prevalence: TP 380, FN 20, TN 300, FP 300, giving PPV ≈ 56% and NPV ≈ 94%. LR+ = 1.9 and LR− = 0.1. This is why D-dimer is used only to rule out PE when probability is low.
- Events fall from 10% to 7.5%: ARR = 2.5%, RRR = 25% and NNT = 40. The same RRR at a baseline of 2% gives ARR 0.5% and NNT 200.

Exam pitfalls
- Saying sensitivity depends on prevalence (predictive values do).
- Giving antithrombotics for 'tearing' pain radiating to the back before excluding dissection.

cards.f: Cardiac output (formula and typical resting value)
cards.b: Cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume. In a resting adult it is roughly 5 L/min (e.g. 70 beats/min x 70 mL).

Within physiological limits, a greater end-diastolic volume (preload) produces a more forceful contraction and a larger stroke volume. Stretch optimises actin-myosin overlap and increases myofilament sensitivity to calcium.

MAP is approximately diastolic pressure + one third of the pulse pressure at resting heart rates. Physiologically, MAP = cardiac output x total peripheral resistance (ignoring the small central venous pressure).

Resistance = 8ηL / πr^4, so resistance is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the radius. Halving an arteriole's radius increases its resistance 16-fold, which is why arterioles control flow and peripheral resistance.

cards.f: Ionic basis of the SA node pacemaker potential
cards.b: Slow depolarisation is driven by the 'funny' current (If, mainly Na+ through HCN channels) and then T-type Ca2+ channels; the upstroke is due to L-type Ca2+ influx (not fast Na+), and repolarisation to K+ efflux.

cards.f: Phases of the ventricular myocyte action potential
cards.b: Phase 0: rapid Na+ influx; phase 1: brief K+ efflux; phase 2: plateau as L-type Ca2+ influx balances K+ efflux; phase 3: repolarisation by K+ efflux; phase 4: stable resting potential (about -90 mV).

cards.f: Why cardiac muscle cannot be tetanised
cards.b: The long plateau gives a long effective refractory period lasting almost until relaxation is complete, so a new action potential cannot summate contractions. This guarantees filling between beats.

Ca2+ entering through L-type channels triggers calcium-induced calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum via ryanodine receptors (RyR2). Ca2+ binds troponin C, allowing cross-bridge cycling; relaxation follows Ca2+ reuptake by SERCA and extrusion by the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger.

cards.f: Function of the AV node delay
cards.b: The AV node conducts slowly (about 0.1 s delay), letting the atria finish emptying before ventricular systole. It also limits how many impulses reach the ventricles when the atrial rate is very fast, e.g. in AF.
Noradrenaline acting on beta1 receptors raises heart rate (steeper pacemaker slope), contractility (more Ca2+ entry and SR uptake), conduction velocity and the rate of relaxation.

Stretch receptors in the carotid sinus (glossopharyngeal nerve) and aortic arch (vagus) signal to the nucleus tractus solitarius. A fall in pressure reduces firing, which increases sympathetic and reduces vagal outflow, raising heart rate, contractility and vasoconstriction.

Net filtration depends on capillary minus interstitial hydrostatic pressure, opposed by plasma minus interstitial oncotic pressure (mainly albumin). Normally slightly more fluid is filtered than reabsorbed and the excess is returned by lymphatics.

cards.f: Why a fall in plasma albumin causes oedema
cards.b: Low albumin reduces plasma oncotic pressure, so the force drawing fluid back into capillaries falls and net filtration rises. When filtration exceeds lymphatic drainage, interstitial fluid accumulates.

cards.f: Coronary perfusion and the cardiac cycle
cards.b: Left ventricular myocardium is perfused mainly in diastole because systolic contraction compresses intramyocardial vessels. Tachycardia shortens diastole and so reduces coronary filling time while increasing oxygen demand.
Cardiac output = oxygen consumption / (arterial O2 content - mixed venous O2 content). For example, 250 mL O2/min divided by 50 mL O2/L gives 5 L/min.

cards.f: Type I vs type II pneumocytes
cards.b: Type I pneumocytes are thin, flat cells covering most of the alveolar surface for gas exchange. Type II pneumocytes secrete surfactant and act as progenitors that regenerate the epithelium after injury.

A phospholipid-protein mixture (mainly dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine) secreted by type II pneumocytes. It lowers alveolar surface tension, increasing compliance, stabilising small alveoli and reducing the tendency to oedema; deficiency causes neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.

cards.f: Law of Laplace applied to alveoli
cards.b: P = 2T/r: with equal surface tension, a smaller alveolus would need a higher pressure to stay open and would empty into larger ones. Surfactant lowers tension more as alveoli shrink, preventing this instability.
Compliance is the change in volume per unit change in distending pressure (ΔV/ΔP). It is reduced in pulmonary fibrosis and oedema (stiff lungs) and increased in emphysema (loss of elastic tissue).

The volume left in the lungs at the end of a quiet expiration (expiratory reserve volume + residual volume). It is the point where the inward recoil of the lungs balances the outward recoil of the chest wall.

cards.f: Anatomical dead space and alveolar ventilation
cards.b: Anatomical dead space (about 150 mL in an adult) is the conducting airway volume that takes no part in gas exchange. Alveolar ventilation = (tidal volume - dead space) x respiratory rate, so rapid shallow breathing is inefficient.

cards.f: Shape of the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve
cards.b: Sigmoid because of cooperative binding: each O2 bound increases the affinity of the remaining haem groups. The flat upper part protects loading despite falls in alveolar PO2; the steep part allows large O2 release at tissue PO2.

cards.f: Factors shifting the O2-Hb curve to the right
cards.b: Raised PCO2, raised H+ (fall in pH), raised temperature and raised 2,3-BPG reduce haemoglobin's O2 affinity, aiding unloading in active tissues. The effect of CO2 and H+ is the Bohr effect.
Most CO2 travels as bicarbonate, formed by carbonic anhydrase in red cells (with chloride shift); smaller fractions are carried as carbamino compounds on haemoglobin and dissolved in plasma.
Deoxygenated haemoglobin carries more CO2 (as carbamino compounds and by buffering H+) than oxygenated haemoglobin. Oxygenation in the lungs therefore promotes CO2 unloading.

Pulmonary arterioles constrict when alveolar PO2 is low, diverting blood to better-ventilated lung and improving V/Q matching. This is the opposite of the systemic response to hypoxia; when generalised (e.g. chronic hypoxia, altitude) it causes pulmonary hypertension.

Central chemoreceptors in the medulla respond to H+ in CSF generated from CO2 and give most of the normal drive to breathe. Peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid and aortic bodies) respond mainly to low PaO2, particularly below about 8 kPa, and also to raised PaCO2 and H+.

cards.f: Fick's law of diffusion across the alveolar membrane
cards.b: Gas transfer is proportional to surface area x diffusion coefficient x partial pressure difference, divided by membrane thickness. Emphysema reduces area; fibrosis increases thickness; both reduce transfer.

cards.f: Regional V/Q in the upright lung
cards.b: Both ventilation and perfusion increase towards the base, but perfusion increases more steeply. So V/Q is high at the apex and low at the base.

cards.f: Muscles of quiet inspiration and expiration
cards.b: Quiet inspiration is active, mainly via the diaphragm (phrenic nerve, C3-C5) with the external intercostals. Quiet expiration is passive elastic recoil; forced expiration recruits abdominal muscles and internal intercostals.

Endothelial dysfunction allows LDL to enter the intima where it is oxidised. Monocytes enter, become macrophages and take up oxidised LDL to form foam cells (fatty streak); smooth muscle cells migrate and lay down collagen to form a fibrous cap over a lipid core.

A thin fibrous cap, large lipid-rich necrotic core and many inflammatory cells (macrophages degrade collagen). Such plaques are prone to rupture, exposing thrombogenic material and causing acute coronary syndrome.

cards.f: Stable angina vs acute coronary syndrome mechanism
cards.b: Stable angina: a fixed narrowing limits flow only when demand rises. ACS: plaque rupture or erosion triggers platelet-rich thrombus that suddenly reduces or occludes flow at rest.

cards.f: Modifiable vs non-modifiable cardiovascular risk factors
cards.b: Modifiable: smoking, hypertension, raised LDL/non-HDL cholesterol, diabetes, obesity, physical inactivity, poor diet, excess alcohol. Non-modifiable: age, male sex, family history of premature CVD, ethnicity (e.g. South Asian background).

A UK risk calculator estimating 10-year risk of heart attack or stroke from factors such as age, sex, ethnicity, deprivation, smoking, BP, cholesterol ratio, BMI, diabetes and certain conditions. NICE uses a 10-year risk of 10% or more as the threshold for offering a statin in primary prevention.
Pack-years = (cigarettes per day / 20) x years smoked. For example, 30 a day for 20 years = 30 pack-years.
Smoking causes endothelial dysfunction and oxidative stress, increases LDL oxidation, raises fibrinogen and platelet activation, and lowers HDL. Carbon monoxide also reduces oxygen delivery.

Usually autosomal dominant, most often a mutation in the LDL receptor gene (also APOB or PCSK9), reducing hepatic LDL clearance. It causes very high LDL from birth, tendon xanthomata and premature coronary disease; first-degree relatives should be tested.

Essential (primary) hypertension, the large majority, has no single identifiable cause. Secondary causes include renal parenchymal disease, renal artery stenosis, primary hyperaldosteronism, phaeochromocytoma, Cushing's syndrome and coarctation of the aorta.
The three factors that predispose to thrombosis: stasis of blood flow, hypercoagulability, and endothelial (vessel wall) injury.

Immobility, recent surgery (especially orthopaedic) or trauma, active cancer, pregnancy and the postpartum period, combined oral contraceptive or HRT, previous VTE, obesity and inherited thrombophilia (e.g. factor V Leiden).

cards.f: Main causes of chronic heart failure in the UK
cards.b: Coronary heart disease is the most common, followed by hypertension; others include valve disease, cardiomyopathies, arrhythmias such as AF, and alcohol.

Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction: EF 40% or less, mainly impaired contraction. Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction: EF 50% or more with impaired relaxation/filling; 41-49% is termed mildly reduced.

An autoimmune sequel of group A streptococcal pharyngitis, in which antibodies cross-react with cardiac antigens (molecular mimicry). Repeated episodes scar valves; mitral stenosis is the classic chronic lesion.

cards.f: Risk factors and organisms in infective endocarditis
cards.b: Risk factors: prosthetic valve, previous endocarditis, structural or congenital heart disease, injecting drug use (often right-sided, tricuspid). Staphylococcus aureus is now the commonest cause; viridans streptococci are associated with poor dental health.
Cigarette smoking is by far the main cause in the UK. Others include occupational dusts and fumes, biomass fuel smoke, and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

Smoke recruits neutrophils and macrophages that release elastase and other proteases, while oxidants inactivate alpha-1 antitrypsin. Unopposed proteolysis destroys alveolar walls, reducing gas-exchange area and elastic recoil.

Centriacinar (centrilobular) emphysema affects the respiratory bronchioles, is typical of smoking and predominates in the upper lobes. Panacinar emphysema involves the whole acinus, is typical of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency and predominates in the lower lobes.

Productive cough on most days for at least 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years, other causes excluded. Pathologically there is mucous gland hypertrophy, goblet cell hyperplasia and airway inflammation.

Sensitised mast cells with IgE degranulate on allergen exposure, releasing histamine and leukotrienes (early bronchoconstriction). Th2 cytokines (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13) drive eosinophilic inflammation and a late-phase response; chronically there is airway remodelling.

Viral respiratory infections, allergens (house dust mite, pollen, animal dander), cold air, exercise, smoke and pollution, and drugs such as beta-blockers and, in some people, aspirin or other NSAIDs.

Autosomal recessive disease of the CFTR chloride channel (commonest variant F508del). Thick, dehydrated secretions cause recurrent infection (e.g. Pseudomonas aeruginosa), bronchiectasis, pancreatic insufficiency and male infertility.
Streptococcus pneumoniae. Others include Haemophilus influenzae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus (notably after influenza) and Legionella.

cards.f: Main risk factors for lung cancer
cards.b: Smoking is the dominant cause; others include radon, asbestos and other occupational carcinogens, air pollution and family history. Adenocarcinoma is now the most common type and the commonest in never-smokers.
Pleural plaques (benign), diffuse pleural thickening, asbestosis (interstitial fibrosis), lung cancer (risk multiplied with smoking) and mesothelioma, which may appear decades after exposure.

cards.f: Abdominal aortic aneurysm: risk factors and screening
cards.b: Risk factors: male sex, older age, smoking (strongest modifiable), hypertension and family history. The NHS offers a one-off ultrasound screen to men in the year they turn 65.

Right ventricular hypertrophy and failure caused by pulmonary hypertension secondary to lung disease or hypoxia (e.g. COPD), driven largely by chronic hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction and vascular remodelling.
Loss of organised atrial contraction leads to stasis, particularly in the left atrial appendage, where thrombus forms and can embolise to the brain.
One small square = 0.04 s; one large square (5 small) = 0.2 s; five large squares = 1 s.
PR interval 0.12-0.20 s (3-5 small squares); QRS duration under 0.12 s (3 small squares); QTc roughly under 0.44-0.46 s, longer in women.

cards.f: Calculating heart rate from an ECG
cards.b: For a regular rhythm: 300 divided by the number of large squares between R waves. For an irregular rhythm: count QRS complexes on a 10-second rhythm strip and multiply by 6.

cards.f: ECG lead groups and coronary territories
cards.b: Inferior (II, III, aVF): usually right coronary artery. Anterior/septal (V1-V4): left anterior descending. Lateral (I, aVL, V5-V6): circumflex or diagonal branches.

New ST elevation at the J point in at least two contiguous leads above set thresholds (1 mm in most leads, higher in V2-V3), or left bundle branch block with ongoing ischaemic symptoms (managed as a STEMI equivalent). Reciprocal ST depression supports the diagnosis.
Irregularly irregular RR intervals, no discernible P waves and an irregular fibrillatory baseline; QRS is usually narrow.
Tall peaked T waves, then flattening or loss of P waves and PR prolongation, then broadening QRS, a sine-wave pattern and ultimately VF or asystole.

FEV1 is the volume exhaled in the first second of a forced expiration from full inspiration; FVC is the total volume exhaled in that manoeuvre. Their ratio distinguishes obstructive from restrictive patterns.

Obstructive: FEV1/FVC below 0.7 (or below the lower limit of normal), e.g. asthma, COPD. Restrictive: FVC reduced with a normal or raised ratio, e.g. pulmonary fibrosis, chest wall or neuromuscular disease.
Spirometry is repeated after an inhaled bronchodilator. A rise in FEV1 of at least 12% and 200 mL is the traditional threshold for significant reversibility, supporting asthma rather than COPD.

Measures CO uptake to reflect gas transfer across the alveolar-capillary membrane. Reduced in emphysema, interstitial lung disease, pulmonary vascular disease (e.g. PE) and anaemia; typically normal or raised in asthma and raised in pulmonary haemorrhage.

cards.f: Normal arterial blood gas values (on air)
cards.b: pH 7.35-7.45; PaO2 about 10-13 kPa; PaCO2 4.7-6.0 kPa; bicarbonate 22-26 mmol/L; base excess -2 to +2.

Type 1: PaO2 below 8 kPa with normal or low PaCO2 (oxygenation failure, e.g. pneumonia, PE). Type 2: PaO2 below 8 kPa with PaCO2 above about 6 kPa (ventilatory failure, e.g. COPD, opioid overdose, neuromuscular weakness).

cards.f: Alveolar gas equation and A-a gradient
cards.b: PAO2 = FiO2 x (atmospheric - water vapour pressure) - PaCO2/0.8; on room air at sea level this is about 20 - PaCO2/0.8 kPa. A-a gradient = PAO2 - PaO2, normally under about 2 kPa in young adults and rising with age; a raised gradient indicates V/Q mismatch, shunt or diffusion impairment.

Assess oxygenation (with FiO2), then pH (acidaemia or alkalaemia), then PaCO2 (respiratory component) and bicarbonate/base excess (metabolic component), decide the primary disturbance and whether compensation is present.
S1 is closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves at the start of systole; S2 is closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves. S2 normally splits on inspiration as the pulmonary valve closes later.

Aortic stenosis: ejection systolic, loudest in the aortic area, radiating to the carotids. Mitral regurgitation: pansystolic at the apex radiating to the axilla. Aortic regurgitation: early diastolic at the left sternal edge. Mitral stenosis: low mid-diastolic rumble at the apex.

Height of the internal jugular pulsation measured vertically above the sternal angle with the patient at 45 degrees; normally up to about 3-4 cm. Raised in right heart failure, fluid overload, tricuspid regurgitation and tamponade; fixed and non-pulsatile in SVC obstruction.
Dull: consolidation, collapse or fibrosis. Stony dull: pleural effusion. Hyper-resonant: pneumothorax (and sometimes hyperinflated emphysematous lungs).
Pushed away from a tension pneumothorax or massive pleural effusion; pulled towards lobar collapse, upper lobe fibrosis or a previous pneumonectomy.

Respiratory: lung cancer, bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, empyema or lung abscess. Cardiac: cyanotic congenital heart disease, infective endocarditis. COPD alone does not cause clubbing, so its presence needs investigation.

If clinic BP is 140/90 mmHg or higher (but below 180/120), offer ambulatory BP monitoring (or home monitoring if ABPM is unsuitable). Stage 1 hypertension is confirmed by a daytime average of 135/85 mmHg or higher.
The bladder should encircle most of the arm (about 80%). A cuff that is too small overestimates BP; one that is too large can underestimate it.

Troponin I or T released from injured myocytes; high-sensitivity assays measured at presentation and repeated show a rise and/or fall in myocardial infarction. Troponin is also raised in PE, myocarditis, sepsis, heart failure and renal failure.

Peptides released by ventricular myocytes in response to wall stretch. A normal level makes heart failure unlikely; a raised level prompts echocardiography and specialist assessment, with urgency set by how high it is.

A fibrin degradation product: highly sensitive but poorly specific for VTE. It is used to rule out DVT/PE in patients with a low (unlikely) clinical probability; it is also raised by infection, surgery, cancer, pregnancy and older age.

Gives no information on CO2 or ventilation; falsely normal in carbon monoxide poisoning; unreliable with poor perfusion, movement or nail varnish; and can overestimate saturation in people with darker skin.
An exaggerated fall in systolic BP of more than 10 mmHg on inspiration. Seen in cardiac tamponade and acute severe asthma.
A large-volume pulse with a rapid upstroke and rapid fall, classically in aortic regurgitation; also in high-output states such as pregnancy, anaemia and thyrotoxicosis.

Beta1 antagonism lowers heart rate, contractility and renin release, reducing myocardial oxygen demand. Used in angina, rate control of AF, after MI and in HFrEF (e.g. bisoprolol); avoided in asthma because beta2 blockade can cause bronchospasm.

cards.f: ACE inhibitors: mechanism and key adverse effects
cards.b: Block conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, causing vasodilation and lower aldosterone; they also reduce bradykinin breakdown. Adverse effects: dry cough, angioedema, hyperkalaemia, first-dose hypotension and renal impairment; contraindicated in pregnancy.
Block the AT1 receptor (e.g. losartan, candesartan) with similar effects to ACE inhibitors. Because bradykinin is not affected, cough is much less common; used when ACE inhibitors are not tolerated.

cards.f: Dihydropyridine vs rate-limiting calcium channel blockers
cards.b: Dihydropyridines (e.g. amlodipine) act mainly on vascular smooth muscle, causing vasodilation with ankle oedema, flushing and headache. Verapamil and diltiazem also slow the SA and AV nodes and are avoided in HFrEF. Verapamil must not be combined with a beta-blocker (risk of severe bradycardia, heart block and hypotension); diltiazem may be used with a beta-blocker only with caution and close monitoring.
Inhibit the Na+/Cl- cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule (e.g. indapamide). Adverse effects: hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hyperuricaemia and gout, hyperglycaemia and erectile dysfunction.

Inhibit the Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter (NKCC2) in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle (e.g. furosemide), causing powerful diuresis. Used to relieve congestion in heart failure; cause hypokalaemia, hypovolaemia and, at high doses, ototoxicity.

Inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting step of cholesterol synthesis. Lower hepatocyte cholesterol upregulates LDL receptors, increasing LDL clearance from blood; adverse effects include muscle aches, rarely myopathy, and raised liver enzymes.

Irreversibly acetylates platelet COX-1, blocking thromboxane A2 production for the platelet's lifespan (about 7-10 days). Used in secondary prevention after MI or ischaemic stroke; main risks are GI and other bleeding.

Block the platelet ADP P2Y12 receptor: clopidogrel and prasugrel (irreversible prodrugs; clopidogrel activation depends on CYP2C19) and ticagrelor (reversible, active drug). Combined with aspirin as dual antiplatelet therapy after ACS or stenting.
Inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, preventing gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X (and proteins C and S). Monitored by the INR; many drug and dietary interactions.
Apixaban, rivaroxaban and edoxaban directly inhibit factor Xa; dabigatran directly inhibits thrombin. No routine INR monitoring is needed, but renal function affects dosing and suitability.

Both enhance antithrombin. Unfractionated heparin inhibits thrombin and factor Xa and needs APTT monitoring; LMWH acts mainly on factor Xa and is given subcutaneously. Both can cause heparin-induced thrombocytopenia; protamine reverses heparin.

Releases nitric oxide, which activates guanylyl cyclase to raise cGMP and relax vascular smooth muscle. Predominant venodilation reduces preload and wall stress, lowering myocardial oxygen demand; never combined with PDE5 inhibitors (severe hypotension).

Inhibits the Na+/K+-ATPase; the resulting rise in intracellular Na+ reduces Ca2+ extrusion via the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger, increasing contractility. It also increases vagal tone, slowing AV conduction, which is why it is used for rate control in AF.

Nausea, vomiting, confusion, visual disturbance (yellow-green tinge) and arrhythmias including heart block and ventricular ectopy. Precipitated by hypokalaemia (e.g. from diuretics), renal impairment and interacting drugs such as amiodarone.

Spironolactone or eplerenone block aldosterone receptors, reducing sodium retention and myocardial fibrosis and improving survival in HFrEF. Main risks are hyperkalaemia and renal impairment; spironolactone can cause gynaecomastia.

Dapagliflozin and empagliflozin block sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 in the proximal tubule. Beyond diabetes, they reduce heart failure hospitalisation and cardiovascular death in HFrEF and are added to standard therapy; NICE also recommends them as an option in HFmrEF and HFpEF.

Combines a neprilysin inhibitor (raising natriuretic peptides) with an ARB. Used in HFrEF in place of an ACE inhibitor or ARB; it must not be taken with an ACE inhibitor because of angioedema risk, so a 36-hour washout is needed.
Short-acting beta2 agonist: Gs activation raises cAMP and PKA activity, relaxing bronchial smooth muscle. Adverse effects include tremor, tachycardia, palpitations and hypokalaemia at high doses.

Act on intracellular glucocorticoid receptors to switch off inflammatory gene transcription, reducing eosinophilic airway inflammation and hyperresponsiveness. Local adverse effects: oral candidiasis and hoarse voice (rinse mouth, use spacer); high doses carry systemic risks.

E.g. tiotropium: block M3 receptors on airway smooth muscle, preventing vagally mediated bronchoconstriction and reducing mucus secretion. A mainstay of COPD therapy; adverse effects include dry mouth and urinary retention.

Under the 2024 NICE/BTS/SIGN asthma guideline, adults and young people (12+) with newly diagnosed asthma are offered an as-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol inhaler rather than a SABA alone. Each reliever dose then also delivers anti-inflammatory steroid.

Montelukast blocks the CysLT1 receptor, opposing leukotriene-mediated bronchoconstriction, mucus secretion and eosinophil recruitment. An add-on option in asthma; neuropsychiatric effects (e.g. sleep disturbance, mood change) are a recognised warning.

A methylxanthine that inhibits phosphodiesterase and antagonises adenosine receptors, giving modest bronchodilation. Narrow therapeutic index: toxicity causes arrhythmias and seizures; levels are altered by smoking and CYP1A2 inhibitors such as ciprofloxacin.

Class I: Na+ channel blockers (e.g. flecainide). Class II: beta-blockers. Class III: K+ channel blockers prolonging repolarisation (e.g. amiodarone, sotalol). Class IV: rate-limiting Ca2+ channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem).

Thyroid dysfunction (hypo- or hyper-), pulmonary fibrosis, liver toxicity, photosensitivity and skin discolouration, corneal deposits, and QT prolongation; its very long half-life prolongs effects and interactions (e.g. with warfarin and digoxin).

Acts on A1 receptors to cause transient AV nodal block, terminating re-entrant SVTs that use the AV node. Its half-life is seconds; it causes brief chest tightness, flushing and a sense of doom and is avoided in asthma.
Most acutely ill adults: 94-98%. Patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure (e.g. COPD with CO2 retention): 88-92%, pending blood gases.
The proportion of people with the disease who test positive: TP / (TP + FN). A highly sensitive test, when negative, helps rule a condition out ('SnNout').
The proportion of people without the disease who test negative: TN / (TN + FP). A highly specific test, when positive, helps rule a condition in ('SpPin').
PPV = TP / (TP + FP); NPV = TN / (TN + FN). Unlike sensitivity and specificity, predictive values depend on prevalence: PPV falls when a test is used in a low-prevalence population.
LR+ = sensitivity / (1 - specificity); LR- = (1 - sensitivity) / specificity. Post-test odds = pre-test odds x likelihood ratio, linking a test result to the probability of disease.

The estimated chance a patient has a condition before a test, based on prevalence, history and examination. The same test result means very different things at different pre-test probabilities, so tests should be chosen and interpreted in that light.

cards.f: Absolute vs relative risk reduction and NNT
cards.b: ARR = control event rate - treated event rate; RRR = ARR / control event rate; NNT = 1 / ARR. A large RRR can mean a tiny ARR when baseline risk is low.
Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure: assess and treat each problem as it is found before moving on, reassessing after every intervention and calling for help early.

The National Early Warning Score 2 aggregates respiratory rate, SpO2 (scale 1 or 2), use of supplemental oxygen, systolic BP, pulse, level of consciousness (ACVPU) and temperature. A total of 5 or more triggers urgent review and 7 or more an emergency response; a score of 3 in any single parameter also prompts urgent review.

Confusion; urea over 7 mmol/L; respiratory rate 30 or more; systolic BP below 90 or diastolic 60 or less; age 65 or over. One point each; it estimates 30-day mortality in community-acquired pneumonia and guides place of care (CRB-65 is used without bloods in the community).

A clinical prediction rule combining items such as signs of DVT, PE being the most likely diagnosis, tachycardia, recent immobilisation or surgery, previous VTE, haemoptysis and cancer. In NICE's two-level version, over 4 = PE likely (go to CTPA); 4 or less = unlikely (do D-dimer first).

Stroke-risk score in AF: Congestive heart failure, Hypertension, Age 75+ (2), Diabetes, previous Stroke/TIA/thromboembolism (2), Vascular disease, Age 65-74, Sex category female. NICE advises offering anticoagulation at a score of 2 or more, considering it in men with a score of 1.

A bleeding-risk tool recommended by NICE (2021) for people with AF considering anticoagulation; it uses haemoglobin/anaemia, age, previous bleeding, renal function and antiplatelet use. It identifies modifiable bleeding risks rather than being a reason on its own to withhold anticoagulation.

cards.f: Life-threatening causes of acute chest pain to exclude
cards.b: Acute coronary syndrome, aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism, tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade and oesophageal rupture.
Check patient details and calibration, then rate, rhythm, axis, P waves, PR interval, QRS width and morphology, ST segments, T waves and QT interval, and compare with previous ECGs.

Anchoring: sticking with an initial impression despite new information. Premature closure: stopping the search once a plausible diagnosis is found. Both are countered by deliberately asking 'what else could this be?'

System 1 is fast, intuitive pattern recognition; System 2 is slow, analytical reasoning. Experts use both, and errors often arise when System 1 is not checked by System 2 in atypical or high-stakes cases.
A structured handover or escalation tool: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation. It makes urgent communication concise and ensures a clear request is made.

A process in which clinician and patient choose tests or treatments together, combining evidence on benefits and harms with the patient's values and preferences. Expected under UK consent law (Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board, 2015) and NICE guidance.

Inability to complete sentences, RR over 30, SpO2 below 92% (or falling), cyanosis, silent chest, exhaustion or drowsiness, hypotension and new confusion: each indicates an emergency needing immediate senior help.
A test's sensitivity and specificity measured in clear-cut cases and healthy controls usually overstates its performance in the mixed, milder patients seen in practice.

questions.q: Which cells secrete pulmonary surfactant?
questions.why: Type II pneumocytes produce and secrete surfactant and can regenerate the alveolar epithelium; type I cells are thin cells specialised for gas exchange.

questions.q: An arteriole constricts so that its radius halves while length and blood viscosity stay the same. By roughly how much does its resistance to flow change?
questions.why: By Poiseuille's law resistance is proportional to 1/r^4, so halving the radius raises resistance by 2^4 = 16 times.

questions.q: Which ionic current is mainly responsible for the upstroke (phase 0) of the sinoatrial node action potential?
options: The funny current (If) through HCN channels
K+ efflux through delayed rectifier channels
questions.why: SA node cells have few functional fast Na+ channels at their resting potential, so their slow upstroke is carried by L-type Ca2+ channels; If drives the earlier pacemaker depolarisation.

questions.q: Explain why the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve is sigmoid, and give two physiological advantages of this shape.
markScheme: Cooperative binding: binding of each O2 molecule changes haemoglobin's conformation (T to R state) and increases the affinity of the remaining haem groups, giving a sigmoid curve.
The flat upper portion means saturation stays high even if alveolar PO2 falls moderately (e.g. altitude, mild lung disease), protecting O2 loading.
The steep middle portion means a small fall in PO2 in the tissues releases a large amount of O2, aiding unloading where it is needed.
questions.modelAnswer: Haemoglobin binds oxygen cooperatively. When one haem group binds O2, the molecule shifts from the tense (T) to the relaxed (R) conformation, raising the affinity of the other haem groups, so saturation rises steeply over a middle range of PO2 and then levels off. The plateau above about 8 kPa means arterial blood remains well saturated even when alveolar PO2 falls somewhat, so loading in the lungs is protected. The steep part, which corresponds to tissue PO2 values, means a small further drop in PO2 in active tissue unloads a large amount of oxygen.

questions.q: A healthy student stands up quickly from lying down. Explain the immediate cardiovascular reflex that prevents her from fainting.
markScheme: On standing, gravity pools around 500 mL of blood in the leg veins, reducing venous return, preload and (by Frank-Starling) stroke volume, so arterial pressure falls.
Reduced stretch of carotid sinus and aortic arch baroreceptors lowers their firing rate (afferents in glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves to the nucleus tractus solitarius).
The medulla increases sympathetic and reduces parasympathetic (vagal) outflow, raising heart rate and contractility.
Sympathetic arteriolar constriction increases total peripheral resistance and venoconstriction restores venous return, so MAP (= CO x TPR) is restored within seconds.
questions.modelAnswer: When she stands, blood pools in the compliant leg veins, so venous return and end-diastolic volume fall. By the Frank-Starling mechanism stroke volume falls, and with it cardiac output and arterial pressure. Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus (via the glossopharyngeal nerve) and aortic arch (via the vagus) are stretched less and fire less, and this is signalled to the nucleus tractus solitarius. The medullary cardiovascular centres respond by reducing vagal tone and increasing sympathetic outflow. Heart rate and contractility rise, arterioles constrict to raise total peripheral resistance, and veins constrict to push blood back towards the heart. Because MAP equals cardiac output times peripheral resistance, pressure is restored within a few beats and cerebral perfusion is maintained.

questions.q: In a patient at rest, oxygen consumption is 300 mL/min, arterial O2 content is 200 mL/L and mixed venous O2 content is 150 mL/L. Calculate the cardiac output. Then explain what would happen to mixed venous O2 content if cardiac output fell while oxygen consumption stayed the same.
markScheme: States the Fick principle: CO = VO2 / (CaO2 - CvO2).
Correct calculation: 300 / (200 - 150) = 300 / 50 = 6 L/min.
If CO falls with constant VO2, each litre of blood must give up more O2, so the arteriovenous O2 difference widens.
Mixed venous O2 content (and saturation) therefore falls, which is why a low mixed venous saturation is a marker of inadequate cardiac output.
questions.modelAnswer: The Fick principle states that oxygen uptake equals blood flow multiplied by the arteriovenous oxygen content difference, so cardiac output = VO2 / (CaO2 - CvO2). Here the difference is 200 - 150 = 50 mL O2 per litre, so cardiac output = 300 / 50 = 6 L/min. If cardiac output fell while the tissues still consumed 300 mL O2 per minute, each litre of blood passing through the tissues would have to give up more oxygen. Tissues achieve this by increasing extraction, so the arteriovenous difference widens and mixed venous O2 content and saturation fall. A low mixed venous saturation therefore signals inadequate oxygen delivery, as in cardiogenic shock.

questions.q:
Priya, a healthy 20-year-old student, flies to Nepal and treks rapidly to 4,500 m. On the evening she arrives she feels breathless on minimal exertion and has a headache. At rest her respiratory rate is 22/min, heart rate 104/min and SpO2 85% on air. An expedition doctor runs an arterial blood gas: pH 7.53, PaO2 6.5 kPa, PaCO2 3.4 kPa, HCO3- 21 mmol/L.

(a) Interpret the blood gas. (b) Explain the mechanism of her increased ventilation and why, on the first day, ventilation does not rise as much as the hypoxaemia alone would drive it. (c) Describe the physiological adaptations that occur over the following days to weeks. (d) Explain why rapid ascent can lead to pulmonary oedema.
markScheme: Interprets ABG: hypoxaemia (PaO2 below 8 kPa) with low PaCO2 and raised pH, i.e. respiratory alkalosis due to hyperventilation; bicarbonate only slightly reduced, consistent with an acute picture (no significant renal compensation yet).
Explains low inspired PO2 at altitude (barometric pressure falls; FiO2 still 21%), so alveolar and arterial PO2 fall.
Peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid bodies, glossopharyngeal nerve) respond to PaO2 below about 8 kPa and drive ventilation.
Hyperventilation lowers PaCO2, CSF H+ falls and central chemoreceptor drive is reduced; the alkalosis also inhibits peripheral chemoreceptors, braking the response.
Over 2-3 days: kidneys excrete bicarbonate and CSF bicarbonate is adjusted, pH normalises and ventilation rises further (ventilatory acclimatisation).

Rise in red cell 2,3-BPG shifts the O2-Hb curve to the right, aiding unloading; erythropoietin from the kidney raises haematocrit over weeks; increased capillary density and mitochondrial adaptations.

Generalised hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction raises pulmonary artery pressure; uneven vasoconstriction exposes some capillaries to high pressure, causing stress failure and leaky, protein-rich oedema (HAPE).
Links practical relevance: gradual ascent allows acclimatisation; descent is the key treatment for altitude illness.
Clear structure addressing each part with correct terminology.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The PaO2 of 6.5 kPa shows significant hypoxaemia. PaCO2 is low and pH is high, so there is a respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation. Bicarbonate is only slightly reduced, as expected from chemical buffering in an acute disturbance; renal compensation has not yet occurred.

(b) At altitude the barometric pressure is lower, so although air is still 21% oxygen the inspired and alveolar PO2 fall. The carotid bodies detect arterial PO2 and their firing rises steeply below about 8 kPa, increasing ventilation via the glossopharyngeal nerve to the medulla. However, the extra ventilation blows off CO2. Lower PaCO2 reduces H+ in the CSF, reducing the drive from the central chemoreceptors, and the alkalaemia also damps the peripheral chemoreceptors. These opposing effects limit the initial rise in ventilation.

(c) Over two to three days the kidneys excrete bicarbonate, bringing blood pH back towards normal, and CSF bicarbonate also falls. The brake on breathing is removed and ventilation rises further, raising alveolar PO2: this is ventilatory acclimatisation. Red cell 2,3-BPG rises, shifting the dissociation curve to the right to aid oxygen unloading. Hypoxia stimulates renal erythropoietin release, so haemoglobin and haematocrit rise over weeks, increasing oxygen content (at the cost of higher viscosity). Tissue capillary density and oxidative capacity also adapt. Heart rate stays raised early on; plasma volume falls, which also concentrates haemoglobin.

(d) Pulmonary arterioles constrict in response to alveolar hypoxia. Locally this improves V/Q matching, but when the whole lung is hypoxic it raises pulmonary artery pressure. Vasoconstriction is uneven, so some capillary beds receive high flow at high pressure; their walls undergo stress failure and leak protein-rich fluid into the alveoli. This high-altitude pulmonary oedema worsens hypoxaemia further. Gradual ascent prevents much of this, and descent is the most effective treatment.

questions.q:
Tom, a 25-year-old motorcyclist, is brought to the emergency department after a collision with a fractured femur and an estimated blood loss of 1.5 litres. He is anxious. Heart rate 126/min, blood pressure 98/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, capillary refill time 4 seconds, peripheries cool and pale. A urinary catheter drains 10 mL in the first hour.

Explain, with reference to underlying physiology: (a) why his pulse pressure is narrow; (b) the short-term neural mechanisms maintaining his blood pressure; (c) the mechanisms that restore circulating volume over minutes to days; and (d) why a 'normal-looking' systolic blood pressure can be falsely reassuring in a young adult with haemorrhage.
markScheme: Haemorrhage reduces venous return and preload; by Frank-Starling, stroke volume falls, so pulse pressure (which depends largely on stroke volume and arterial compliance) narrows.
Diastolic pressure is maintained or rises because of sympathetic arteriolar constriction (raised TPR), further narrowing pulse pressure.
Baroreceptor unloading increases sympathetic and decreases vagal outflow: tachycardia, increased contractility, arteriolar constriction (skin, gut, kidney), maintaining MAP = CO x TPR.
Venoconstriction mobilises blood from capacitance veins to support venous return; adrenaline release from adrenal medulla.
Explains the clinical signs: cool, pale peripheries and prolonged capillary refill reflect cutaneous vasoconstriction; tachypnoea and anxiety reflect sympathetic activation and reduced perfusion.
Capillary Starling forces: reduced capillary hydrostatic pressure (arteriolar constriction, lower venous pressure) favours reabsorption of interstitial fluid into plasma ('autotransfusion').
Renal hypoperfusion and sympathetic stimulation release renin: angiotensin II (vasoconstriction, thirst, aldosterone) and aldosterone (Na+ and water retention); low urine output.
ADH (vasopressin) release triggered by reduced atrial/baroreceptor stretch causes water retention and vasoconstriction; red cells replaced over weeks via erythropoietin.
Young adults compensate so effectively that hypotension appears late (often after substantial loss); tachycardia, narrow pulse pressure, CRT, oliguria and mental state are earlier markers of shock.
Coherent, well-organised answer linking each mechanism to the observations.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Losing 1.5 litres reduces venous return and ventricular filling. By the Frank-Starling relationship, a lower end-diastolic volume gives a smaller stroke volume. Pulse pressure depends mainly on stroke volume and arterial compliance, so it falls. At the same time sympathetic arteriolar constriction raises peripheral resistance and supports diastolic pressure, so the gap between systolic and diastolic (98/78, pulse pressure 20 mmHg) narrows.

(b) Lower arterial pressure reduces stretch of carotid sinus and aortic arch baroreceptors. The medulla responds with less vagal and more sympathetic outflow. Heart rate and contractility rise, partly offsetting the fall in stroke volume. Arterioles in skin, gut, muscle and kidneys constrict, raising total peripheral resistance, so MAP (cardiac output x TPR) is protected and flow is diverted to the brain and heart. Veins constrict, pushing blood from the capacitance vessels towards the heart. The adrenal medulla releases adrenaline. These effects explain his cool, pale skin, prolonged capillary refill and anxiety.

(c) Arteriolar constriction and lower venous pressure reduce capillary hydrostatic pressure. Oncotic pressure is initially unchanged, so the Starling balance favours reabsorption of interstitial fluid into the plasma, restoring some volume within minutes to hours. Reduced renal perfusion and sympathetic stimulation of the juxtaglomerular cells release renin. Angiotensin II constricts vessels, stimulates thirst and releases aldosterone, which increases sodium and water reabsorption. Reduced stretch of atrial and arterial receptors triggers ADH release, increasing water reabsorption in the collecting ducts and causing vasoconstriction. His low urine output reflects these mechanisms and reduced renal perfusion. Plasma proteins are replaced by the liver over days, and red cells over weeks through erythropoietin.

(d) Fit young adults can keep systolic pressure near normal until a large share of their blood volume is lost, because these reflexes are so effective. A systolic of 98 mmHg can look acceptable, but the tachycardia, narrow pulse pressure, prolonged capillary refill, tachypnoea and oliguria show significant hypovolaemic shock. When compensation fails, pressure can fall suddenly. So he needs urgent haemorrhage control and blood replacement, not reassurance from his systolic reading.

questions.q:
Josh, a tall, thin 22-year-old who smokes, develops sudden right-sided pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness while sitting at his desk. Respiratory rate 24/min, heart rate 102/min, SpO2 93% on air, blood pressure 124/78 mmHg. The trachea is central. On the right there is reduced chest expansion, hyper-resonant percussion and quiet breath sounds. A chest X-ray shows a right-sided pneumothorax with a visible lung edge.

(a) Explain the normal pressures and forces that keep the lung expanded within the chest wall. (b) Explain why air entering the pleural space causes the lung to collapse, and account for each examination finding. (c) Explain why his oxygen saturation is reduced. (d) Explain what would distinguish a tension pneumothorax physiologically and clinically, and why it is immediately life-threatening.
markScheme: Lung elastic recoil (elastic fibres plus surface tension) pulls inwards while the chest wall tends to spring outwards; at FRC these balance.
This creates a subatmospheric (negative) intrapleural pressure, about -0.5 kPa (-5 cmH2O) at FRC, which holds the visceral pleura against the parietal pleura via a thin fluid layer.

A breach (here likely rupture of an apical bleb/bulla, typical of tall thin young men and smokers) lets air enter until intrapleural pressure approaches atmospheric; the lung recoils inwards and the chest wall springs slightly outwards.

Explains signs: reduced expansion on the affected side; hyper-resonance from air in the pleural space; quiet breath sounds because air insulates sound and the lung is not ventilated; central trachea in a simple pneumothorax.
Reduced SpO2: perfusion continues to the collapsed, poorly ventilated lung, causing V/Q mismatch/shunt; hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction partly limits this. Tachypnoea and pain contribute.
Tension pneumothorax: a one-way valve lets air in on inspiration but not out, so intrapleural pressure rises above atmospheric.

Mediastinal shift away from the affected side (tracheal deviation away), compression of the opposite lung and kinking/compression of great veins reduce venous return and cardiac output: tachycardia, hypotension, distended neck veins, rising hypoxaemia.
Recognises tension pneumothorax as a clinical diagnosis requiring immediate needle decompression/thoracostomy before imaging.
Well-structured answer with correct pressure terminology.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The lungs have an inherent tendency to recoil inwards because of elastic fibres and alveolar surface tension, while the chest wall tends to spring outwards. At functional residual capacity these opposing forces balance. Because the two pleural layers are separated only by a thin film of fluid, they cannot easily separate, and the opposing pulls create a subatmospheric intrapleural pressure of about -0.5 kPa (around -5 cmH2O) at FRC. This negative pressure holds the lung expanded against the chest wall, and it becomes more negative when the inspiratory muscles expand the thorax.

(b) In primary spontaneous pneumothorax a small apical bleb usually ruptures; this is commoner in tall, thin young men and in smokers. Air enters the pleural space until intrapleural pressure approaches atmospheric pressure. The force holding the lung out is lost, so the lung recoils towards the hilum and the chest wall springs slightly outwards. The right side moves less because the lung under it is not inflating. Air in the pleural space gives a hyper-resonant percussion note. Breath sounds are quiet because the collapsed lung is poorly ventilated and air in the pleural space does not transmit sound well. In a simple pneumothorax the mediastinum is not pushed across, so the trachea is central.

(c) Blood keeps flowing through the partly collapsed lung even though it is poorly ventilated. This blood returns to the left heart without full oxygenation, creating low V/Q areas and shunt that lower arterial saturation. Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction diverts some flow to the ventilated lung and limits the fall. Pain and anxiety contribute to his tachypnoea.

(d) In a tension pneumothorax the breach acts as a one-way valve. Air enters with each breath but cannot leave, so intrapleural pressure rises above atmospheric. The mediastinum is pushed to the opposite side: the trachea deviates away, the other lung is compressed, and the great veins are compressed or kinked. Venous return and cardiac output fall, giving severe tachycardia, hypotension, distended neck veins and worsening hypoxaemia, which can lead to cardiac arrest. It is a clinical diagnosis and needs immediate decompression without waiting for an X-ray.

questions.q:
Ellie, a 19-year-old university rower, takes part in a laboratory exercise test. Measurements:

At rest: heart rate 60/min, stroke volume 80 mL, oxygen consumption 0.30 L/min, arterial O2 content 200 mL/L.
At peak exercise: heart rate 190/min, stroke volume 130 mL, oxygen consumption 4.0 L/min, arterial O2 content 200 mL/L. Arterial PO2 and PCO2 are close to resting values throughout moderate exercise.

(a) Calculate her cardiac output and mixed venous O2 content at rest and at peak exercise. (b) Explain the mechanisms that increase stroke volume and heart rate. (c) Explain how blood flow is redistributed and how oxygen extraction by working muscle increases. (d) Explain how ventilation is matched to metabolism so that arterial gases stay stable. (e) Evaluate whether the cardiovascular or the respiratory system is more likely to limit maximal oxygen uptake in a healthy young athlete.
markScheme: Rest: CO = 60 x 0.08 = 4.8 L/min; a-v difference = 300/4.8 = 62.5 mL/L, so mixed venous content about 137.5 mL/L.
Peak: CO = 190 x 0.13 = 24.7 L/min; a-v difference = 4000/24.7 = about 162 mL/L, so mixed venous content about 38 mL/L (extraction rises from about 31% to about 81%).
Heart rate: withdrawal of vagal tone then sympathetic stimulation (beta1, steeper pacemaker slope) and circulating adrenaline.

Stroke volume: increased contractility from sympathetic stimulation (more Ca2+ entry and SR uptake) and increased venous return/preload via the skeletal muscle pump, respiratory pump and venoconstriction (Frank-Starling); faster relaxation preserves filling despite tachycardia.

Redistribution: local metabolic vasodilation in working muscle (raised K+, H+, CO2, adenosine, low O2, NO) overrides sympathetic tone (functional sympatholysis); sympathetic constriction in gut, kidney and inactive tissue; skin flow rises later for heat loss.
Total peripheral resistance falls, so MAP rises only modestly despite the large rise in CO; systolic rises, diastolic stable or falls.

Increased extraction: capillary recruitment (shorter diffusion distance, larger surface area), lower muscle PO2 steepening the gradient, rightward shift of the O2-Hb curve from raised PCO2 and H+ (the Bohr effect) and from raised temperature; myoglobin assists intracellular transfer.

Ventilation rises with increased tidal volume then rate; driven by central command and feedback from muscle and joint receptors, with chemoreceptor fine-tuning; alveolar ventilation rises in proportion to CO2 production so PaCO2 stays stable. Above the anaerobic (lactate) threshold, ventilation rises disproportionately and PaCO2 falls.

Evaluation: in healthy people, oxygen delivery (maximal cardiac output) is the main limit; ventilatory reserve remains at peak and arterial saturation is maintained in most people. Acknowledges exceptions (e.g. exercise-induced arterial hypoxaemia in some elite athletes, lung disease, muscle mitochondrial capacity).
Well-organised, correctly calculated, with units throughout.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Cardiac output is heart rate x stroke volume. At rest it is 60 x 0.080 L = 4.8 L/min. By the Fick principle the arteriovenous O2 difference is VO2/CO = 300/4.8 = 62.5 mL/L, so mixed venous content is about 137.5 mL/L (about 31% extraction). At peak exercise CO = 190 x 0.130 = 24.7 L/min, and the difference is 4000/24.7, about 162 mL/L, so mixed venous content is about 38 mL/L (about 81% extraction). The roughly 13-fold rise in VO2 comes from a five-fold rise in cardiac output combined with a much wider extraction.

(b) Heart rate rises first through withdrawal of vagal tone and then through sympathetic beta1 stimulation and circulating adrenaline, which steepen the pacemaker potential. Stroke volume rises because sympathetic stimulation increases contractility, with more calcium entering and faster uptake into the SR, and because preload is maintained or raised. Rhythmic muscle contraction squeezes blood through the veins (the muscle pump), deeper breathing lowers intrathoracic pressure (the respiratory pump) and venoconstriction mobilises blood, so the Frank-Starling mechanism also contributes. Faster relaxation helps the ventricles fill despite the short diastole.

(c) In working muscle, local metabolites (K+, H+, CO2, adenosine, low PO2, nitric oxide) dilate arterioles and override sympathetic constriction. Gut, kidney and inactive muscle receive less flow through sympathetic vasoconstriction, while skin flow later rises to lose heat. Total peripheral resistance falls, so mean pressure rises only modestly. Extraction rises because more capillaries open, which increases surface area and shortens diffusion distance. Muscle PO2 falls, steepening the gradient. Local rises in PCO2 and H+ (the Bohr effect), together with the rise in temperature, shift the dissociation curve to the right, unloading more oxygen.

(d) Ventilation rises with metabolism through central command and feedback from muscle and joint receptors, with chemoreceptors fine-tuning it. Alveolar ventilation rises in proportion to CO2 production, so PaCO2 and PaO2 stay near normal. Above the lactate threshold, buffering of lactic acid adds CO2 and H+, ventilation rises more steeply and PaCO2 falls.

(e) In healthy people, the main limit to maximal oxygen uptake is how much oxygen the circulation can deliver, set by maximal cardiac output. At peak exercise there is usually spare ventilatory capacity and arterial saturation is maintained. Some elite endurance athletes, though, show exercise-induced arterial desaturation because transit time through pulmonary capillaries becomes very short. Muscle oxidative capacity also contributes. In lung disease the balance shifts and ventilation may become limiting.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the components of Virchow's triad?
questions.why: Virchow's triad is stasis, hypercoagulability and vessel wall injury; a low platelet count usually increases bleeding risk rather than defining thrombosis risk.

questions.q: A 58-year-old woman with lower-lobe-predominant panacinar emphysema has never smoked. Which underlying condition is most likely?
questions.why: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency leaves neutrophil elastase unopposed, typically causing panacinar, lower-zone emphysema, often earlier and in people with little or no smoking history.

questions.q: Which feature makes an atherosclerotic coronary plaque most likely to rupture and cause an acute coronary syndrome?
options: A thick, collagen-rich fibrous cap with a small lipid core
Heavy, uniform calcification of the plaque
A thin fibrous cap over a large lipid-rich necrotic core with many macrophages
A plaque causing a fixed 80% stenosis on angiography
questions.why: Vulnerable plaques have thin caps weakened by macrophage proteases over a large necrotic core; many plaques that rupture were not severely stenosing beforehand.

questions.q: List three modifiable and three non-modifiable risk factors for coronary heart disease.
markScheme: First mark: any two valid modifiable factors (smoking, hypertension, raised LDL/non-HDL cholesterol, diabetes, obesity, physical inactivity, poor diet, excess alcohol).
Second mark for a full correct set of three modifiable factors.
Three valid non-modifiable factors: increasing age, male sex, family history of premature CVD, ethnicity (e.g. South Asian background).
questions.modelAnswer: Modifiable risk factors are those a person or treatment can change: cigarette smoking, hypertension and raised LDL or non-HDL cholesterol are the classic three; diabetes, obesity, physical inactivity and excess alcohol also contribute. Non-modifiable risk factors include increasing age, male sex, a family history of premature cardiovascular disease in a first-degree relative, and ethnicity, with people of South Asian background at higher risk in the UK. These factors interact, so overall risk is assessed with tools such as QRISK3.

questions.q: Explain how cigarette smoking leads to emphysema, and why this reduces expiratory airflow even though emphysema is a disease of the alveoli.
markScheme: Smoke recruits and activates neutrophils and macrophages in the lung, which release proteases such as neutrophil elastase and matrix metalloproteinases.
Oxidants in smoke inactivate alpha-1 antitrypsin, so the protease-antiprotease balance tips towards destruction of alveolar walls (permanent enlargement of airspaces distal to terminal bronchioles).
Loss of elastic tissue reduces lung elastic recoil, which is the driving pressure for passive expiration.
Loss of alveolar attachments (radial traction) means small airways collapse during forced expiration (dynamic airway compression), causing air trapping and a low FEV1/FVC.
questions.modelAnswer: Tobacco smoke recruits neutrophils and macrophages to the lungs, and these release elastase and other proteases. Smoke oxidants also inactivate alpha-1 antitrypsin, the main protective antiprotease, so proteolysis goes unchecked. Alveolar walls are destroyed, producing permanently enlarged airspaces. Although the damage is alveolar, it reduces airflow in two ways. First, loss of elastic fibres lowers elastic recoil, the pressure that drives passive expiration. Second, alveolar walls normally tether small airways open by radial traction. Without them, small airways collapse early in forced expiration as pleural pressure becomes positive, trapping air. The result is obstructive spirometry with a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio and hyperinflation.

questions.q: A 34-year-old man's father died of a myocardial infarction at 46. The son has a total cholesterol of 9.2 mmol/L and thickened Achilles tendons. Suggest the most likely diagnosis, explain its molecular basis and how it causes premature atherosclerosis, and state why his relatives should be assessed.
markScheme: Diagnosis: familial hypercholesterolaemia (tendon xanthomata, very high cholesterol, family history of premature CHD).
Usually autosomal dominant; most often mutations in the LDL receptor gene (also APOB or PCSK9 gain-of-function).
Reduced hepatic LDL receptor-mediated uptake raises plasma LDL from birth.
Lifelong high LDL exposure drives LDL entry and oxidation in the arterial intima, foam cell formation and early plaque development, so coronary events occur decades early.
Autosomal dominant inheritance means each first-degree relative has a 50% chance; cascade testing allows early statin treatment and risk reduction.
questions.modelAnswer: The most likely diagnosis is heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia. Most cases are caused by mutations in the LDL receptor gene, with others in APOB (reducing receptor binding) or gain-of-function PCSK9 (increasing receptor breakdown). Fewer working hepatic LDL receptors mean LDL is cleared slowly and plasma levels are high from birth. Lifelong high LDL means more LDL enters and is oxidised in the arterial intima, where macrophages form foam cells, so plaques develop and coronary disease appears decades early. Inheritance is autosomal dominant, so each first-degree relative has a 50% chance; cascade testing finds affected relatives, including children, so they can start lipid-lowering treatment early.

questions.q:
Derek, a 62-year-old taxi driver, presents with central chest tightness on walking uphill, relieved within 5 minutes by rest. He has smoked 20 cigarettes a day since the age of 17, has type 2 diabetes and hypertension, and his brother had a myocardial infarction at 52. BMI 33 kg/m2, blood pressure 156/94 mmHg. Total cholesterol 6.8 mmol/L, HDL 0.9 mmol/L. Resting ECG is normal.

(a) Calculate his smoking history in pack-years. (b) Explain the pathogenesis of the lesion most likely responsible for his symptoms, linking each of his risk factors to the process. (c) Explain why his pain comes on with exertion and settles with rest, and why his resting ECG can be normal. (d) Explain how this condition could progress to a myocardial infarction.
markScheme: Pack-years: 20/20 x 45 years = 45 pack-years.
Diagnosis of stable angina due to atherosclerotic coronary artery stenosis.
Endothelial dysfunction/injury initiates the process: hypertension (shear and pressure stress), smoking (oxidants, reduced NO), hyperglycaemia/diabetes (glycation, oxidative stress).
LDL enters the intima and is oxidised; raised LDL/total cholesterol and low HDL (less reverse cholesterol transport) promote lipid accumulation.

Monocytes adhere (adhesion molecules), become macrophages and form foam cells; smooth muscle cells migrate and proliferate, forming a fibrous cap over a lipid core; obesity contributes via insulin resistance, dyslipidaemia and inflammation; family history indicates genetic susceptibility.

Fixed stenosis limits coronary flow reserve: exertion raises heart rate, contractility and wall stress, increasing O2 demand beyond supply, causing ischaemia; tachycardia also shortens diastole (perfusion time).
At rest supply meets demand, so there is no ischaemia and the ECG is often normal; ischaemic changes (e.g. ST depression) may appear only during exertion.

Progression: plaque rupture or erosion exposes collagen and tissue factor, causing platelet adhesion and aggregation, coagulation and thrombus formation, which may occlude the artery (STEMI) or partly obstruct it (NSTEMI/unstable angina); prolonged ischaemia leads to necrosis.
Clear organisation and accurate pathology terminology.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Pack-years = (cigarettes per day / 20) x years smoked = (20/20) x 45 = 45 pack-years.

(b) His history fits stable angina from atherosclerotic narrowing of a coronary artery. Atherosclerosis starts with endothelial dysfunction. Hypertension adds mechanical stress, smoking adds oxidants and lowers nitric oxide, and hyperglycaemia causes glycation and oxidative stress. The damaged endothelium lets LDL into the intima, where it is oxidised. His high total cholesterol and low HDL favour lipid build-up, because HDL normally carries cholesterol back to the liver. Activated endothelium expresses adhesion molecules that recruit monocytes. These become macrophages, take up oxidised LDL and become foam cells, forming a fatty streak. Cytokines and growth factors make smooth muscle cells migrate into the intima and lay down collagen, forming a fibrous cap over a lipid-rich core. Obesity contributes through insulin resistance, dyslipidaemia and low-grade inflammation, and his brother's early MI suggests inherited susceptibility. As the plaque grows it narrows the lumen.

(c) At rest a moderately narrowed artery can still supply enough blood. Climbing a hill raises heart rate, contractility and wall stress, so myocardial oxygen demand rises. Normally the coronary arterioles dilate to increase flow, but beyond a fixed stenosis this reserve is already used up, so supply cannot rise to match. Tachycardia also shortens diastole, when most left ventricular perfusion happens. The resulting ischaemia causes pain, partly through adenosine and other metabolites stimulating cardiac afferents. Rest lowers demand and the ischaemia resolves. Because there is no ischaemia at rest, the resting ECG is often normal; ST depression may only show during exercise.

(d) If the fibrous cap ruptures or the endothelium erodes, collagen and tissue factor are exposed. Platelets adhere and aggregate and the coagulation cascade forms a thrombus. A thrombus that fully occludes the artery causes a STEMI. One that partly blocks it gives unstable angina or NSTEMI. Ischaemia lasting more than about 20-30 minutes leads to myocyte necrosis.

questions.q:
Maureen, a 68-year-old retired school cook, is admitted with breathlessness. She smoked 25 cigarettes a day for 45 years. For several years she has had a cough productive of white sputum every winter morning. Over the past 6 months her ankles have become swollen. On examination she is centrally cyanosed, with a raised JVP, a parasternal heave, loud P2 and bilateral pitting ankle oedema.
