Arterial blood gas on air: pH 7.38, PaO2 7.1 kPa, PaCO2 7.0 kPa, HCO3- 31 mmol/L. Haemoglobin 182 g/L. Spirometry: FEV1/FVC 0.48, FEV1 38% predicted.

(a) Interpret her blood gas and spirometry. (b) Explain how her smoking caused her lung disease. (c) Explain the mechanism of her ankle oedema and cardiac signs. (d) Explain her raised haemoglobin. (e) Discuss why her oedema is not due to left ventricular failure, and what investigation would help confirm this.
markScheme: Spirometry: FEV1/FVC below 0.7 = obstruction; FEV1 38% predicted = severe COPD (GOLD 3 range: 30-49%).
ABG: hypoxaemia with hypercapnia (type 2 respiratory failure), normal pH with raised HCO3-: chronic, compensated respiratory acidosis (renal bicarbonate retention).

Smoking pathogenesis: chronic bronchitis (mucous gland hypertrophy, goblet cell hyperplasia, impaired mucociliary clearance, small airway inflammation and fibrosis) and emphysema (protease-antiprotease imbalance, loss of recoil); 56 pack-years.
Chronic alveolar hypoxia causes generalised hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction and vascular remodelling, producing pulmonary hypertension; hypercapnia/acidosis worsens vasoconstriction.
Raised pulmonary pressure causes right ventricular hypertrophy (parasternal heave, loud P2) and eventually right heart failure: cor pulmonale.

Raised right-sided/venous pressure increases capillary hydrostatic pressure, raising filtration and causing peripheral oedema and raised JVP; reduced renal perfusion and hypercapnia also promote salt and water retention via RAAS.
Raised Hb: chronic hypoxaemia stimulates renal erythropoietin release, causing secondary polycythaemia, which increases O2 content but raises viscosity and pulmonary vascular resistance.

Evaluation: no orthopnoea/PND or crackles given; signs are right-sided; pulmonary hypertension from lung disease explains them. Echocardiography would show RV dilatation/hypertrophy, raised estimated pulmonary artery pressure and preserved LV function; BNP may be raised in both so is less discriminating.
Notes caution with oxygen therapy (target 88-92%) given CO2 retention.
Logical structure integrating physiology and clinical findings.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The FEV1/FVC of 0.48 shows airflow obstruction, and an FEV1 of 38% predicted is severe, which in her smoking context fits COPD. The ABG shows hypoxaemia (PaO2 7.1 kPa) with hypercapnia (PaCO2 7.0 kPa), i.e. type 2 respiratory failure. pH is normal and bicarbonate is raised, so the kidneys have retained bicarbonate over time: this is a chronic, compensated respiratory acidosis.

(b) She has a 56 pack-year history. Smoke causes mucous gland hypertrophy and goblet cell hyperplasia and damages cilia, giving her chronic productive cough (chronic bronchitis), together with inflammation and fibrosis of small airways. It also drives protease release and inactivates alpha-1 antitrypsin, destroying alveolar walls (emphysema). Recoil falls and small airways collapse on expiration. Mismatched ventilation and perfusion, together with a high work of breathing, lead to hypoxaemia and then CO2 retention.

(c) Chronic alveolar hypoxia causes widespread hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, worsened by hypercapnic acidosis. Over time the pulmonary arterioles remodel, producing pulmonary hypertension. The right ventricle hypertrophies against the higher afterload, which gives the parasternal heave, and the loud P2 reflects forceful pulmonary valve closure. Eventually the right ventricle fails (cor pulmonale). Systemic venous pressure rises, raising the JVP and capillary hydrostatic pressure in dependent tissues, so filtration exceeds lymphatic drainage and pitting oedema develops. Hypercapnia and activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system also promote salt and water retention.

(d) Chronic hypoxaemia stimulates erythropoietin release from the kidney, producing secondary polycythaemia. This raises oxygen-carrying capacity but also blood viscosity, which adds to pulmonary vascular resistance.

(e) There are no features of left ventricular failure such as orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea or basal crackles. Her signs are right-sided and are explained by lung disease causing pulmonary hypertension. Echocardiography would help: it would show a dilated, hypertrophied right ventricle with a raised estimated pulmonary artery pressure but preserved left ventricular function. Natriuretic peptides can rise in either condition, so they discriminate less well. Because she retains CO2, controlled oxygen with a target of 88-92% is appropriate.

questions.q: "Most cases of chronic lung disease and heart disease in the UK are preventable." Discuss this statement with reference to COPD, asthma, coronary heart disease and lung cancer. In your answer, distinguish between causes and risk factors, consider the roles of genetic susceptibility, the environment and social deprivation, and evaluate the strengths and limits of prevention at the level of the individual and of the population.
markScheme: Defines terms: a cause is necessary or sufficient (or a component of a sufficient cause); a risk factor is associated with increased probability and may or may not be causal; introduces modifiable vs non-modifiable.

COPD: smoking is the dominant cause in the UK, so most cases are in principle preventable; notes occupational exposures, air pollution, early-life factors (low birth weight, childhood infection) and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency; not all smokers develop COPD (susceptibility).

Asthma: strong genetic/atopic component with gene-environment interaction; primary prevention is limited, but exacerbations and deaths are often preventable (inhaler technique, adherence, avoiding triggers, anti-inflammatory therapy).

Coronary heart disease: a few modifiable factors (smoking, BP, lipids, diabetes, obesity, inactivity) account for most population risk, but age, sex, family history and ethnicity are not modifiable; familial hypercholesterolaemia shows genetics can be modified by treatment.
Lung cancer: smoking causes the large majority of UK cases; radon, asbestos and air pollution contribute; a sizeable minority arise in never-smokers, especially adenocarcinoma.

Social deprivation: higher smoking rates, poorer housing (damp, mould, overcrowding), occupational exposures and poorer access to care produce a steep social gradient; prevention must address structural determinants.

Individual approach (high-risk strategy): risk scoring (e.g. QRISK3) and statins, BP control, smoking cessation support; strengths are targeted benefit; limits include that most events occur in the many at moderate risk, adherence, overmedicalisation.

Population approach (Rose's prevention paradox): small shifts in risk across a population prevent more cases than intensive treatment of high-risk individuals; examples include smoke-free legislation, tobacco taxation, clean air policies.

Evaluates 'preventable': distinguishes preventable in principle from preventable in practice, notes lag times (lung cancer decades after exposure), residual risk and the difference between preventing onset and preventing progression or death.
Balanced conclusion supported by argument; clear essay structure.
questions.modelAnswer:
The statement is broadly true, but 'preventable' needs careful definition. A cause is a factor without which a given case would not have occurred, often as one component of a sufficient set. A risk factor is any characteristic associated with higher probability of disease, which may or may not be causal. Prevention works by removing causal, modifiable factors.

COPD fits the statement best. In the UK most cases are caused by smoking, so in principle most could be prevented. Even so, only a minority of smokers develop clinically significant COPD, so susceptibility matters, and occupational dusts, air pollution, early-life lung growth and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency also play a part. Lung cancer is similar: smoking causes the large majority of cases, and radon and asbestos add risk. A significant minority of cases, often adenocarcinoma, occur in never-smokers and are not obviously preventable. The decades-long lag between exposure and disease means today's prevention mostly benefits the future.

Coronary heart disease is driven largely by a few modifiable factors: smoking, blood pressure, lipids, diabetes, obesity and inactivity. Age, sex, family history and ethnicity cannot be changed, but familial hypercholesterolaemia shows that genetic risk can still be reduced by treatment. Asthma fits the statement least well. Its onset reflects strong genetic and atopic susceptibility interacting with environment, and primary prevention is limited. Yet many exacerbations and deaths are preventable through anti-inflammatory therapy, good inhaler technique and trigger avoidance.

Deprivation runs through all four conditions. Smoking, damp housing, hazardous jobs and poorer access to care cluster in poorer areas, producing steep social gradients. Prevention therefore cannot depend on individual choice alone.

Individual-level prevention, such as QRISK3-guided statins, blood pressure control and smoking cessation support, gives large benefits to high-risk people but reaches only those who are identified and adherent. Rose's prevention paradox shows that most cases arise in the large number of people at moderate risk, so population measures (smoke-free laws, tobacco taxation, clean air policy, food reformulation) may prevent more disease overall, even though each person gains little.

In conclusion, much of this disease is preventable in principle, but how far depends on the condition, and in practice prevention is limited by susceptibility, time lags and social structure.

questions.q: On a standard 12-lead ECG recorded at 25 mm/s, the RR interval in a regular rhythm is 4 large squares. What is the heart rate?
questions.why: Heart rate = 300 / number of large squares between R waves = 300 / 4 = 75 beats/min.

questions.q: Spirometry shows FEV1 2.1 L (55% predicted), FVC 2.5 L (54% predicted), FEV1/FVC 0.84. Which pattern does this most suggest?
options: Restrictive defect such as pulmonary fibrosis
questions.why: Both FEV1 and FVC are reduced in proportion, so the ratio is normal or high: a restrictive pattern, which needs confirmation with lung volumes.

questions.q: A 26-year-old has an ABG on air: pH 7.25, PaO2 12.8 kPa, PaCO2 3.0 kPa, HCO3- 10 mmol/L. What is the primary disturbance?
questions.why: The low pH and low bicarbonate indicate a primary metabolic acidosis; the low PaCO2 is compensatory hyperventilation (e.g. diabetic ketoacidosis).

questions.q: Describe the ECG features of atrial fibrillation and explain the physiological basis of each, including why the pulse is irregular and why there may be a pulse deficit.
markScheme: Absent P waves: no organised atrial depolarisation; chaotic atrial activity replaces it.
Irregular fibrillatory baseline (f waves): multiple disorganised wavelets of atrial activity.
Irregularly irregular RR intervals: the AV node receives impulses chaotically and conducts them irregularly; QRS usually narrow because ventricular conduction is normal.
Pulse deficit: beats after short RR intervals have little filling time, lower stroke volume, and may not produce a palpable radial pulse, so the apical rate exceeds the radial rate.
questions.modelAnswer: In atrial fibrillation organised atrial depolarisation is replaced by many chaotic wavelets, so there are no P waves and the baseline shows irregular fibrillatory waves. The AV node is bombarded with impulses at several hundred per minute and conducts them irregularly, depending on its refractory state, so the RR intervals are irregularly irregular. Ventricular conduction itself is usually normal, so the QRS is narrow. Ventricular filling varies with each RR interval: after a short interval the ventricle has little time to fill and stroke volume is small. Some of these beats are too weak to be felt at the wrist, so the apical rate counted with a stethoscope exceeds the radial rate (a pulse deficit).

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman with no prior history has an ABG on air: pH 7.49, PaO2 9.0 kPa, PaCO2 3.6 kPa. Using the simplified alveolar gas equation (PAO2 approximately 20 - PaCO2/0.8 kPa on room air), calculate her A-a gradient, interpret it, and give two possible causes.
markScheme: A-a gradient = 15.5 - 9.0 = 6.5 kPa.
This is raised (normal under about 2 kPa in a young adult), indicating a gas exchange problem rather than hypoventilation.
Notes respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation; her PaO2 looks only mildly low because hyperventilation raises alveolar PO2.
Two plausible causes of V/Q mismatch, shunt or diffusion impairment, e.g. pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, early pulmonary oedema, pneumothorax, asthma.
questions.modelAnswer: Her alveolar PO2 is about 20 - 3.6/0.8 = 20 - 4.5 = 15.5 kPa, so the A-a gradient is 15.5 - 9.0 = 6.5 kPa. In a 30-year-old the gradient should be under about 2 kPa, so this is markedly raised. The high pH and low PaCO2 show an acute respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation. Hyperventilating raises alveolar PO2, so a PaO2 of 9.0 kPa is much worse than it looks and points to a problem with gas exchange (V/Q mismatch, shunt or diffusion impairment) rather than hypoventilation. Possible causes include pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, pneumothorax, early pulmonary oedema or acute asthma; her history and further tests such as a chest X-ray and risk assessment for PE would help decide.

questions.q: Compare the typical findings of chest examination in (i) right lower lobe consolidation, (ii) a large right pleural effusion and (iii) a right-sided pneumothorax. For each, explain the physical basis of the percussion note and breath sounds.
markScheme: Consolidation: expansion reduced on the right, trachea central, percussion dull because airspaces are filled with fluid/exudate.
Consolidation: bronchial breath sounds (and increased vocal resonance) because solid lung transmits sound from patent bronchi well; crackles may be heard.
Effusion: stony dull percussion due to fluid between lung and chest wall; trachea central or deviated away if massive.

Effusion: reduced or absent breath sounds and vocal resonance because fluid separates the lung from the stethoscope and damps transmission (bronchial breathing may be heard just above the fluid level).
Pneumothorax: hyper-resonant percussion because air fills the pleural space.
Pneumothorax: reduced or absent breath sounds and vocal resonance because air poorly transmits sound and the lung is collapsed; trachea central unless tension (away).
questions.modelAnswer: In right lower lobe consolidation, expansion is reduced, the trachea is central, and exudate-filled alveoli give a dull note. Solid lung transmits sound from patent bronchi well, giving bronchial breathing, increased vocal resonance and often crackles. In a large pleural effusion, percussion is stony dull because fluid lies between lung and chest wall. The fluid damps sound, so breath sounds and vocal resonance are reduced or absent; a massive effusion may push the trachea away. In a pneumothorax, air in the pleural space makes the note hyper-resonant. Air transmits sound poorly and the lung beneath is collapsed, so breath sounds and vocal resonance are reduced. The trachea is central unless there is tension, when it deviates away.

questions.q:
Aisha, a 24-year-old law student, attends with episodic wheeze and cough, worse at night and when she cycles in cold weather. She had eczema as a child, and her mother has hay fever. Between episodes she feels well. Examination today is normal. Spirometry: FEV1 2.4 L (72% predicted), FVC 3.6 L (98% predicted), FEV1/FVC 0.67. Fifteen minutes after inhaled salbutamol: FEV1 2.9 L. Her fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) is 62 ppb.

(a) Interpret the spirometry, including a calculation of reversibility. (b) Explain the pathophysiology of her symptoms and of the test results. (c) Explain why spirometry can be normal in asthma and how this affects diagnostic reasoning. (d) Briefly explain how inhaled salbutamol produced the change in FEV1.
markScheme: FEV1/FVC 0.67 is below 0.7, showing obstruction; FVC normal.
Reversibility: rise of 0.5 L = 500 mL; 500/2400 = about 21%, exceeding the 12% and 200 mL thresholds: significant reversibility supporting asthma.
Atopic background (eczema, family atopy) and variability/nocturnal and trigger-related symptoms support asthma.

Pathophysiology: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation (histamine, leukotrienes) causing bronchoconstriction, mucosal oedema and mucus; Th2 cytokines (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13) drive eosinophilic inflammation; airway hyperresponsiveness to cold air/exercise.

FeNO: raised (50 ppb or more is a positive test in adults under the 2024 NICE/BTS/SIGN guideline) reflects IL-13-induced nitric oxide synthase in airway epithelium, i.e. eosinophilic/type 2 airway inflammation.
Nocturnal worsening linked to circadian rise in vagal tone, lower cortisol and adrenaline at night and allergen exposure (bedding).

Asthma is variable: spirometry between episodes may be normal; a normal result does not exclude it; diagnosis combines history with tests showing inflammation or variability (FeNO, reversibility, peak flow variability, bronchial challenge).
Salbutamol: beta2 agonist, Gs-coupled, raises cAMP and PKA, lowering intracellular Ca2+ and myosin light chain phosphorylation, relaxing airway smooth muscle.
Organised answer showing correct calculation and reasoning.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The FEV1/FVC of 0.67 is below 0.7 with a normal FVC, which is an obstructive pattern. After salbutamol FEV1 rose by 0.5 L (500 mL), which is 500/2400, about 21%. This exceeds the usual thresholds of 12% and 200 mL, showing significant reversibility. In a young atopic woman with variable, nocturnal and trigger-related symptoms, this strongly supports asthma.

(b) Her personal history of eczema and her mother's hay fever suggest an atopic tendency. When she inhales an allergen, IgE on sensitised mast cells crosslinks and the cells release histamine and cysteinyl leukotrienes. These cause smooth muscle contraction, mucosal oedema and mucus secretion, all of which narrow the airways and produce wheeze, cough and a low FEV1. Th2 lymphocytes release IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13, which drive IgE production, eosinophil recruitment and a late-phase reaction. Chronic inflammation makes the airways hyperresponsive, so cold air and exercise also trigger narrowing; cooling and drying of the airway mucosa are thought to cause mediator release. Nocturnal symptoms reflect circadian changes: vagal tone is higher and circulating cortisol and adrenaline are lower at night. IL-13 induces nitric oxide synthase in the airway epithelium, so her FeNO of 62 ppb indicates eosinophilic (type 2) inflammation.

(c) Asthma is variable. Between episodes, airway calibre may be normal and so may spirometry. A normal result therefore does not exclude asthma. The diagnosis rests on a compatible history combined with objective evidence of inflammation (FeNO, eosinophil count) or variable obstruction (reversibility, peak flow variability, or bronchial challenge testing if doubt remains).

(d) Salbutamol stimulates beta2 receptors on airway smooth muscle. These are Gs-coupled, so adenylyl cyclase raises cAMP and activates protein kinase A. This lowers intracellular calcium and reduces myosin light chain kinase activity, relaxing the muscle and widening the airway, so FEV1 rose within minutes.

questions.q:
Brian, a 71-year-old retired engineer with hypertension, presents with 6 months of worsening breathlessness. He now sleeps on three pillows and wakes at night gasping. Pulse 96/min, irregularly irregular; BP 148/88 mmHg; JVP raised 6 cm above the sternal angle; displaced apex beat in the sixth intercostal space, anterior axillary line; a third heart sound; fine bibasal inspiratory crackles; pitting oedema to the mid-shins. ECG: atrial fibrillation, ventricular rate about 100/min, with large QRS voltages in the chest leads. NT-proBNP is markedly raised. Chest X-ray: cardiomegaly, upper lobe venous diversion, bilateral small pleural effusions.

(a) Explain how each clinical and investigation finding arises physiologically. (b) Explain how chronic hypertension could have led to his presentation. (c) Explain how the onset of atrial fibrillation could have worsened his symptoms. (d) State what further investigation is essential and what you would expect it to show.
markScheme: Orthopnoea: lying flat increases venous return to a failing left ventricle, raising pulmonary venous and capillary pressure; PND reflects redistribution of fluid at night and reduced adrenergic drive during sleep.
Crackles and upper lobe diversion: raised pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure causes interstitial and alveolar fluid; pleural effusions from raised capillary pressure.
Raised JVP and peripheral oedema: raised right-sided filling pressures (biventricular failure) and salt/water retention through RAAS activation increase capillary hydrostatic pressure.
Displaced apex beat and cardiomegaly: left ventricular dilatation; S3: rapid early diastolic filling into a dilated, stiff or volume-loaded ventricle.
NT-proBNP: released by stretched ventricular myocytes; promotes natriuresis and vasodilation as a counter-regulatory response.
Large QRS voltages: left ventricular hypertrophy from chronic pressure load.

Hypertension: raised afterload causes concentric LVH, raising myocardial O2 demand and stiffness (diastolic dysfunction); hypertension also accelerates coronary atherosclerosis and ischaemia; over time, myocyte loss, fibrosis and dilatation produce systolic failure.

AF: loss of atrial contraction (which matters most in a stiff hypertrophied ventricle) reduces filling; fast irregular rate shortens diastole, reducing filling and coronary perfusion; can cause tachycardia-mediated LV dysfunction; increases stroke risk.

Essential investigation: transthoracic echocardiography: expect LV dilatation and/or hypertrophy, reduced or preserved EF, raised filling pressures, enlarged left atrium, and to look for valve disease.
Well-organised, linking compensatory neurohormonal mechanisms (sympathetic, RAAS, ADH) to fluid retention.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The left ventricle cannot pump the blood it receives, so left atrial and pulmonary venous pressures rise. Raised pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid into the interstitium and alveoli, giving fine bibasal crackles, upper lobe venous diversion and effusions on X-ray. Lying flat returns more blood from the legs and abdomen to the heart, which the failing ventricle cannot handle, so pulmonary pressures rise further and he needs three pillows (orthopnoea). Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea follows gradual reabsorption of oedema while he lies down, together with lower adrenergic drive during sleep. Low cardiac output activates the sympathetic system, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and ADH. These retain salt and water, raising venous pressure, so the JVP is raised and pitting oedema forms, worsened by raised right-sided pressures. A dilated ventricle displaces the apex beat and causes cardiomegaly. The S3 reflects rapid early diastolic filling of a dilated, high-pressure ventricle. Stretched ventricular myocytes release NT-proBNP. High QRS voltages suggest left ventricular hypertrophy.

(b) Years of hypertension raise afterload, and the ventricle responds with concentric hypertrophy. Hypertrophied muscle is stiff and relaxes poorly, which raises filling pressures (diastolic dysfunction). It also needs more oxygen while having relatively less capillary supply. Hypertension speeds up coronary atherosclerosis, adding ischaemic damage. Over time myocyte loss and fibrosis lead to dilatation and impaired contraction, and neurohormonal activation drives further adverse remodelling.

(c) A stiff, hypertrophied ventricle depends heavily on the atrial contribution to late filling. AF removes this. A fast, irregular ventricular rate also shortens diastole, reducing filling and coronary perfusion, so cardiac output falls and filling pressures rise. A persistently fast rate can itself impair LV function, and AF adds stroke risk.

(d) Transthoracic echocardiography is essential. I would expect left ventricular hypertrophy and/or dilatation, an enlarged left atrium, raised filling pressures, and an ejection fraction that defines whether this is HFrEF or HFpEF. It would also look for valve disease.

questions.q:
Sanjay, a 45-year-old accountant, collapses at work and is brought to the emergency department. He is drowsy and confused. Respiratory rate 32/min and deep, heart rate 118/min, BP 96/60 mmHg, SpO2 97% on 2 L/min nasal oxygen. His capillary glucose reads 'HI'. A colleague says he has had type 1 diabetes since childhood and has been vomiting for 2 days. Arterial blood gas on 2 L/min oxygen: pH 7.08, PaO2 14.5 kPa, PaCO2 2.3 kPa, HCO3- 5 mmol/L. Na+ 132 mmol/L, Cl- 96 mmol/L, K+ 5.9 mmol/L. His ECG shows sinus tachycardia with tall T waves.

(a) Interpret the ABG step by step, including the anion gap. (b) Explain why he is breathing deeply and quickly, naming the receptors and pathways involved. (c) Assess whether his respiratory compensation is appropriate, using Winter's formula (expected PaCO2 in kPa approximately 0.2 x HCO3- + 1.1, plus or minus 0.3). (d) Explain the ECG findings and why his total body potassium is likely to be depleted despite the high serum level. (e) Discuss the limitations of relying on SpO2 in this patient.
markScheme: Oxygenation adequate on supplemental O2 (PaO2 14.5 kPa on 2 L/min; should be interpreted relative to FiO2).
pH 7.08 = severe acidaemia; HCO3- 5 = metabolic acidosis; PaCO2 2.3 = low, i.e. respiratory compensation.

Anion gap = Na+ - (Cl- + HCO3-) = 132 - (96 + 5) = 31 mmol/L (raised; normal about 8-12 without K+), indicating unmeasured anions: ketoacids (beta-hydroxybutyrate, acetoacetate) in diabetic ketoacidosis.

Kussmaul breathing: raised H+ stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid bodies) quickly; central chemoreceptors respond more slowly as CSF pH changes; increased tidal volume and rate to blow off CO2.
Winter's: 0.2 x 5 + 1.1 = 2.1 kPa (range about 1.8-2.4); measured 2.3 kPa is within range, so compensation is appropriate and there is no additional respiratory disorder.
Notes that compensation never fully corrects pH, and that tiring or drowsiness could lead to inadequate compensation (rising PaCO2), a warning sign.
Tall T waves reflect hyperkalaemia; acidosis and insulin deficiency shift K+ out of cells (H+/K+ exchange, reduced Na+/K+-ATPase activity), and hyperosmolality draws K+ out with water.

Total body K+ is depleted by osmotic diuresis and vomiting; once insulin and fluids are given, K+ moves back into cells and serum K+ can fall dangerously, so close monitoring and replacement are needed.

SpO2 limitations: 97% says nothing about ventilation, CO2 or acid-base status; supplemental oxygen can mask deterioration; acidosis shifts the O2-Hb curve right; poor perfusion (hypotension, cool peripheries) can give unreliable readings; ABG/VBG is essential.
Hypotension and tachycardia reflect hypovolaemia from osmotic diuresis and vomiting; prioritises ABCDE resuscitation and senior help.
Systematic, well-reasoned structure.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Oxygenation: his PaO2 of 14.5 kPa is adequate on 2 L/min, though it has to be judged against the oxygen he is breathing. pH 7.08 is severe acidaemia. Bicarbonate of 5 mmol/L shows a primary metabolic acidosis, and the low PaCO2 of 2.3 kPa is respiratory compensation. The anion gap is Na+ - (Cl- + HCO3-) = 132 - (96 + 5) = 31 mmol/L, well above the usual 8-12 mmol/L. This means unmeasured anions have accumulated, here ketoacids (beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate). With a very high glucose in a person with type 1 diabetes, the picture is diabetic ketoacidosis.

(b) The excess H+ stimulates the carotid body chemoreceptors, which signal through the glossopharyngeal nerve to the medullary respiratory centres. Central chemoreceptors respond more slowly as CSF pH changes. Tidal volume and rate both rise (Kussmaul breathing), blowing off CO2 so that the PaCO2/HCO3- ratio, and therefore pH, moves back towards normal.

(c) Winter's formula predicts PaCO2 = 0.2 x 5 + 1.1 = 2.1 kPa (about 1.8-2.4). His measured 2.3 kPa lies within this range, so compensation is appropriate and there is no separate respiratory disorder. Compensation never fully corrects pH, though. If he tires or becomes more drowsy, PaCO2 may rise, which would be an ominous sign.

(d) Tall T waves reflect hyperkalaemia. Insulin normally drives K+ into cells through the Na+/K+-ATPase. Without it, and with H+ entering cells in exchange for K+ and hyperosmolality drawing water and K+ out of cells, potassium shifts into the plasma. Meanwhile osmotic diuresis from glycosuria and two days of vomiting have lost large amounts of potassium, so total body stores are depleted. Once insulin and fluids are given, K+ re-enters cells and serum levels can fall quickly, risking arrhythmias, so potassium needs close monitoring and replacement according to protocol.

(e) An SpO2 of 97% is reassuring only about haemoglobin saturation. It says nothing about ventilation, CO2 or the life-threatening acidosis, and supplemental oxygen can hide deterioration. Hypotension and peripheral vasoconstriction can make readings unreliable. A blood gas is essential, alongside ABCDE resuscitation with fluids and early senior involvement.

questions.q: What is the primary molecular target of statins?
questions.why: Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in hepatic cholesterol synthesis, which upregulates LDL receptors and lowers plasma LDL.

questions.q: A woman develops a persistent dry cough a few weeks after starting ramipril for hypertension. What is the most likely mechanism?
options: Accumulation of bradykinin because ACE also breaks down kinins
Angiotensin II accumulation in the lungs
questions.why: ACE (kininase II) degrades bradykinin; inhibiting it lets bradykinin and related mediators accumulate, sensitising airway cough reflexes. Switching to an ARB usually resolves it.

questions.q: A 70-year-old taking bisoprolol for angina is started on verapamil by mistake. Which adverse effect is the main concern?
questions.why: Both drugs depress SA and AV nodal function and contractility; together they can cause severe bradycardia, heart block, hypotension and heart failure, so verapamil must not be combined with a beta-blocker.

questions.q: A man with heart failure taking digoxin is started on high-dose furosemide. A week later he has nausea, confusion and frequent ventricular ectopics. Which change most directly explains his increased sensitivity to digoxin?
options: Hyperkalaemia increasing digoxin binding to Na+/K+-ATPase
Hypokalaemia increasing digoxin binding to Na+/K+-ATPase
questions.why: Digoxin competes with K+ for its binding site on the Na+/K+-ATPase, so diuretic-induced hypokalaemia increases digoxin binding and toxicity; dehydration and reduced renal clearance can add to this.

questions.q: Explain how low-dose aspirin reduces the risk of arterial thrombosis, and why its antiplatelet effect lasts much longer than the drug remains in the blood.
markScheme: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates (inactivates) cyclo-oxygenase-1 in platelets.
This blocks synthesis of thromboxane A2, a potent platelet activator/aggregator and vasoconstrictor, reducing platelet aggregation and arterial (platelet-rich) thrombus formation.
Platelets have no nucleus, so they cannot synthesise new COX-1; inhibition lasts for the platelet's lifespan (about 7-10 days) even after aspirin has been cleared.
Endothelial cells can make new COX, so prostacyclin (anti-aggregatory) production recovers, helping explain why low doses are effective; main adverse effect is bleeding, particularly GI.
questions.modelAnswer: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates cyclo-oxygenase-1 in platelets, blocking the production of thromboxane A2. Thromboxane A2 normally amplifies platelet activation, promotes aggregation and constricts vessels, so blocking it reduces the formation of platelet-rich arterial thrombi such as those that cause myocardial infarction and ischaemic stroke. Because platelets have no nucleus they cannot make new enzyme, so each exposed platelet is inhibited for the rest of its 7-10 day life, even though aspirin itself is cleared from blood within hours. Nucleated endothelial cells can resynthesise COX and recover prostacyclin production, which is one reason low doses are preferred. Its main adverse effect is bleeding, especially from the gastrointestinal tract.

questions.q: Explain the mechanism by which sublingual glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) relieves an attack of angina, and explain two of its common adverse effects or limitations.
markScheme: GTN is converted to nitric oxide, which activates soluble guanylyl cyclase in vascular smooth muscle, raising cGMP and causing relaxation.

Predominant venodilation reduces venous return, preload and LV wall stress, lowering myocardial O2 demand; it also dilates large coronary arteries and relieves spasm (and some arterial dilation reduces afterload).
Headache and flushing from cerebral and cutaneous vasodilation; postural hypotension/dizziness (so take sitting down).

Tolerance with continuous exposure (hence a nitrate-free interval for long-acting nitrates), or the dangerous interaction with PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil), which also raise cGMP and can cause severe hypotension.
questions.modelAnswer: GTN is a nitric oxide donor. Nitric oxide activates soluble guanylyl cyclase in vascular smooth muscle, raising cGMP, which lowers intracellular calcium and relaxes the muscle. Acting mainly on veins, venous pooling reduces venous return and ventricular filling, lowering wall stress and so myocardial oxygen demand, which is the main way it relieves angina. It also dilates large epicardial coronary arteries and reverses spasm. Vasodilation causes headache, flushing and dizziness, so patients should sit to take it. It must not be used with PDE5 inhibitors such as sildenafil, which also raise cGMP and can cause profound hypotension. Continuous exposure causes tolerance, which is why long-acting nitrates need a daily nitrate-free period.

questions.q: Beta-blockers were once avoided in heart failure because they reduce contractility, yet certain beta-blockers (e.g. bisoprolol) are now a core treatment for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. Explain this apparent paradox.
markScheme: In HFrEF, sustained sympathetic activation is initially compensatory but becomes harmful: it raises heart rate and O2 demand, causes myocyte toxicity/apoptosis, arrhythmias and adverse remodelling.
Beta-blockade lowers heart rate, lengthening diastole, improving filling and coronary perfusion and reducing myocardial O2 demand.
Beta1 blockade reduces renin release, dampening RAAS activation (and its fluid retention and remodelling effects).
Reduces the risk of ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death; over months, reverse remodelling can improve ejection fraction; survival benefit shown in large trials.

Explains the practical consequence: started at low dose in stable patients and titrated slowly, because the acute negative inotropic effect can transiently worsen symptoms; not started during acute decompensation.
questions.modelAnswer: In HFrEF, sympathetic activation supports output short term but becomes harmful when sustained. It raises heart rate and oxygen demand, causes calcium overload and myocyte death, promotes arrhythmias and drives remodelling, so the ventricle dilates further. Beta-blockers interrupt this cycle. Slowing the heart lengthens diastole, improving filling and coronary perfusion and lowering oxygen demand. Blocking beta1 receptors on juxtaglomerular cells reduces renin release, damping the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. They also reduce ventricular arrhythmias and sudden death, and over months they allow reverse remodelling with improved ejection fraction; large trials have shown lower mortality. Because their acute negative inotropic effect can briefly worsen symptoms, they are started low in stable patients and titrated slowly.

questions.q:
Leah, a 19-year-old with known asthma, arrives in the emergency department after 2 days of a cold and worsening wheeze despite frequent use of her blue inhaler. She can only speak in short phrases. Respiratory rate 28/min, heart rate 118/min, SpO2 93% on air, peak expiratory flow 45% of her best. Widespread expiratory wheeze is heard. Her ABG on air: pH 7.47, PaO2 8.9 kPa, PaCO2 4.1 kPa.

The team gives oxygen, nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium, and oral prednisolone.

(a) Classify the severity of this attack and justify your answer. (b) Explain the mechanism of action of each of the drugs given and why each is used. (c) Explain one important adverse effect of repeated high-dose salbutamol. (d) Explain why, if a repeat blood gas an hour later showed a PaCO2 of 5.6 kPa with no clinical improvement, this would be alarming even though the value is within the normal range.
markScheme: Acute severe asthma: PEF 33-50% of best, RR 25/min or more, HR 110/min or more, unable to complete sentences.
No life-threatening features yet: SpO2 not below 92%, PaO2 not below 8 kPa, PaCO2 low not normal/raised, no silent chest, exhaustion or altered consciousness.
Oxygen: corrects hypoxaemia from V/Q mismatch (mucus plugging, bronchoconstriction), target 94-98%.
Salbutamol: beta2 agonist, Gs, raised cAMP/PKA, relaxes bronchial smooth muscle; rapid onset; nebulised (oxygen-driven) in severe attacks.
Ipratropium: short-acting muscarinic (M3) antagonist, blocks vagally mediated bronchoconstriction; adds bronchodilation when given with a beta2 agonist in severe attacks.

Prednisolone: glucocorticoid receptor-mediated suppression of inflammatory gene transcription (cytokines, eosinophil survival), reducing airway inflammation and oedema over hours and preventing relapse; also upregulates beta2 receptors.
Salbutamol adverse effect: hypokalaemia (stimulates Na+/K+-ATPase, shifting K+ into cells), risking arrhythmias; also tachycardia, tremor, lactic acidosis.

Rising PaCO2: in acute asthma, hyperventilation should keep PaCO2 low; a 'normal' or rising value with persisting obstruction means fatigue and inadequate alveolar ventilation, a life-threatening feature needing urgent senior/critical care involvement.
Clearly structured answer using correct terminology.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) This is acute severe asthma. Her peak flow is 45% of her best (in the 33-50% band), her respiratory rate is 25/min or more, her heart rate is 110/min or more and she cannot complete sentences. She has no life-threatening features yet: SpO2 is not below 92%, PaO2 is above 8 kPa, PaCO2 is low rather than normal, and there is no silent chest, exhaustion, cyanosis or confusion. The low PaCO2 and raised pH show she is hyperventilating.

(b) Oxygen corrects hypoxaemia caused by V/Q mismatch from bronchoconstriction and mucus plugging, aiming for 94-98%. Salbutamol is a short-acting beta2 agonist. Stimulating Gs-coupled receptors on airway smooth muscle raises cAMP and activates protein kinase A, reducing intracellular calcium and relaxing the muscle within minutes; it is nebulised, driven by oxygen. Ipratropium is a short-acting muscarinic antagonist. It blocks M3 receptors, preventing vagally mediated bronchoconstriction and adding to the effect of salbutamol in severe attacks. Prednisolone acts on intracellular glucocorticoid receptors to switch off transcription of inflammatory genes such as Th2 cytokines, reducing eosinophilic inflammation, mucosal oedema and mucus. Its effect takes hours to develop, but it speeds recovery and reduces relapse; it also upregulates beta2 receptors.

(c) Repeated high-dose salbutamol stimulates the Na+/K+-ATPase in skeletal muscle and shifts potassium into cells, causing hypokalaemia that can provoke arrhythmias, so potassium should be checked. Tachycardia, tremor and lactic acidosis are other effects.

(d) In an acute attack, the drive to breathe should keep PaCO2 below normal, as it was at first. If PaCO2 rises to 5.6 kPa without clinical improvement, she is no longer moving enough air: she is tiring and alveolar ventilation is failing. A normal or raised PaCO2 is a life-threatening feature of acute asthma. It needs immediate senior review, escalation of treatment and early critical care involvement, because respiratory arrest can follow.

questions.q:
Winston, a 58-year-old bus driver of African-Caribbean family origin, has a clinic blood pressure of 162/98 mmHg. Ambulatory monitoring confirms a daytime average of 152/96 mmHg. He does not have diabetes; his eGFR and urine albumin:creatinine ratio are normal and his ECG is normal. His 10-year QRISK3 score is 14%.

(a) Explain how sustained hypertension damages the heart, brain, kidneys and eyes. (b) Following NICE guidance, which drug class would usually be offered first, and why might it be particularly suitable for him? Explain its mechanism. (c) Six weeks later he has bilateral ankle swelling with no breathlessness. Explain the mechanism and why a diuretic is unlikely to help. (d) His BP remains above target. Discuss the options for a second drug, explaining their mechanisms. (e) Outline the other measures that would reduce his overall cardiovascular risk.
markScheme: Target organ damage: LVH and heart failure, accelerated coronary atherosclerosis; stroke (ischaemic and haemorrhagic), vascular dementia; nephrosclerosis and CKD; hypertensive retinopathy.
NICE: for people of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin without type 2 diabetes (and anyone aged 55 or over without diabetes), first step is a calcium channel blocker.
Rationale: average responses to RAAS blockers alone are smaller in this group (often lower-renin hypertension), while CCBs and diuretics are effective; notes individual variation.
Mechanism: dihydropyridine CCB (e.g. amlodipine) blocks L-type Ca2+ channels in arteriolar smooth muscle, causing vasodilation and lower peripheral resistance.

Ankle oedema: preferential precapillary arteriolar dilation raises capillary hydrostatic pressure, increasing filtration; it is not due to salt and water retention, so diuretics are of little benefit; options are dose reduction or adding an ACEi/ARB, which dilates venules.

Second step: add an ACE inhibitor or ARB, or a thiazide-like diuretic (e.g. indapamide); NICE suggests considering an ARB in preference to an ACE inhibitor in people of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin (higher angioedema risk with ACEi).

Mechanisms of ARB (AT1 blockade, reduced vasoconstriction and aldosterone) and thiazide-like diuretic (DCT Na+/Cl- cotransporter inhibition, initial volume reduction then fall in peripheral resistance); monitoring of U&Es.
Lifestyle: salt reduction, weight loss, exercise, limiting alcohol and caffeine, smoking cessation, diet (e.g. DASH-style).
QRISK3 of 14% (10% or more): offer a statin (atorvastatin) for primary prevention after discussion; shared decision-making and adherence.
Well-structured answer with appropriate caution about individual variation.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Raised pressure increases left ventricular afterload, causing concentric hypertrophy, stiffness, diastolic dysfunction and eventually heart failure. Raised wall stress and endothelial damage speed up atherosclerosis, raising the risk of coronary disease. In the brain, hypertension is the most important modifiable risk factor for both ischaemic and haemorrhagic stroke, and it contributes to small-vessel disease and vascular dementia. In the kidneys, arteriolar sclerosis and glomerular hypertension cause nephrosclerosis and chronic kidney disease, which in turn worsens hypertension. In the eyes it causes hypertensive retinopathy.

(b) NICE recommends a calcium channel blocker first for adults of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin without type 2 diabetes, as for anyone aged 55 or over. On average, RAAS blockers given alone lower blood pressure less in this group, which may reflect a tendency to lower-renin hypertension, whereas CCBs work well. Individual responses vary. A dihydropyridine such as amlodipine blocks L-type calcium channels in arteriolar smooth muscle, reducing calcium entry and causing vasodilation that lowers peripheral resistance.

(c) Dihydropyridines dilate precapillary arterioles more than venules, so capillary hydrostatic pressure rises and filtration increases in dependent tissues. There is no salt and water overload, so a diuretic does little. Options are reducing the dose or adding an ACE inhibitor or ARB, which dilates postcapillary vessels and often reduces the oedema.

(d) The second step is to add an ACE inhibitor or ARB, or a thiazide-like diuretic. NICE suggests considering an ARB rather than an ACE inhibitor in people of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin, partly because they have a higher risk of ACE inhibitor-induced angioedema. ARBs block angiotensin II at AT1 receptors, reducing vasoconstriction and aldosterone-driven sodium retention; electrolytes and renal function need checking. Thiazide-like diuretics such as indapamide inhibit the Na+/Cl- cotransporter in the distal tubule, lowering volume at first and peripheral resistance later; they can cause hypokalaemia and hyponatraemia.

(e) Lifestyle measures include salt reduction, weight loss, regular exercise, moderating alcohol and a healthy diet. With a QRISK3 of 14%, above the 10% threshold, he should be offered a statin for primary prevention through shared decision-making. Long-term adherence and regular review are essential.

questions.q:
Gareth, a 57-year-old builder, is treated for an anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction with primary percutaneous coronary intervention and a drug-eluting stent in the left anterior descending artery. Echocardiography before discharge shows mild left ventricular systolic impairment. He is discharged on: aspirin, ticagrelor, high-intensity atorvastatin, bisoprolol and ramipril, with sublingual GTN for chest pain.

For each regular medicine, explain (a) its mechanism of action, (b) the rationale for its use after myocardial infarction, and (c) one important adverse effect or monitoring requirement. Then (d) explain why dual antiplatelet therapy is given for a limited period rather than indefinitely, and (e) suggest two non-drug interventions that would reduce his risk of a further event.
markScheme: Aspirin: irreversible COX-1 inhibition, reduced thromboxane A2; prevents platelet-rich thrombus at the stent and elsewhere; adverse effect GI bleeding (consider PPI cover).
Ticagrelor: reversible P2Y12 (ADP receptor) antagonist; combined with aspirin prevents stent thrombosis and recurrent ACS; adverse effects bleeding and dyspnoea.
Statin: HMG-CoA reductase inhibition, increased LDL receptor expression, lower LDL; also plaque stabilisation (pleiotropic effects); monitor lipids and liver enzymes, ask about muscle symptoms.

Bisoprolol: beta1 antagonism reduces heart rate, contractility and O2 demand; reduces ischaemia and arrhythmias after MI and benefits LV dysfunction; adverse effects bradycardia, fatigue, cold peripheries; caution in asthma.

Ramipril: ACE inhibition reduces angiotensin II and aldosterone; limits adverse ventricular remodelling after MI, especially with LV impairment; monitor U&Es (creatinine, K+) and BP; cough, angioedema.
Explains why stent and ruptured plaque are pro-thrombotic until the stent is endothelialised, so DAPT is most valuable early.

DAPT duration: bleeding risk accumulates over time while thrombotic benefit falls; usually up to 12 months then single antiplatelet continues lifelong; duration individualised by bleeding vs ischaemic risk.
Notes possible addition of a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist if he develops heart failure with significantly reduced EF, and that ticagrelor/aspirin combination needs bleeding counselling.
Non-drug: cardiac rehabilitation, smoking cessation, Mediterranean-style diet, physical activity, weight loss, alcohol moderation, return-to-work and driving advice (DVLA).
Clear, organised answer using correct pharmacological terminology.
questions.modelAnswer:
Aspirin irreversibly inhibits platelet COX-1 and so blocks thromboxane A2 production. After MI it reduces recurrent coronary thrombosis and stent thrombosis and is continued lifelong. Its main risk is bleeding, especially gastrointestinal, and gastroprotection with a proton pump inhibitor is often given alongside dual antiplatelet therapy.

Ticagrelor reversibly blocks the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor. Together with aspirin it gives dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT), which strongly protects the new stent and reduces recurrent ACS. It increases bleeding and can cause breathlessness.

Atorvastatin inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, so hepatocytes express more LDL receptors and plasma LDL falls. Intensive LDL lowering slows plaque progression and stabilises plaques, reducing further events. Lipids and liver enzymes are checked after starting, and he should report muscle pain.

Bisoprolol is a cardioselective beta1 antagonist. It lowers heart rate, contractility and oxygen demand, reduces ischaemia and ventricular arrhythmias, and benefits LV systolic dysfunction. It can cause bradycardia, fatigue and cold peripheries, and it should be avoided in asthma.

Ramipril inhibits ACE, lowering angiotensin II and aldosterone. After MI, particularly with LV impairment, it limits adverse remodelling and reduces heart failure and death. Renal function, potassium and blood pressure are monitored after starting and after dose changes; cough and angioedema are recognised effects.

(d) The ruptured plaque and the newly implanted stent are highly thrombogenic until the stent struts are covered by endothelium, so DAPT gives the most benefit in the early months. Bleeding risk keeps adding up the longer both drugs are taken, while the extra protection declines. DAPT is therefore usually given for up to 12 months, adjusted to his bleeding and ischaemic risk, before continuing a single antiplatelet. If he developed heart failure with a significantly reduced ejection fraction, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist might be added.

(e) Non-drug measures include cardiac rehabilitation (exercise, education and psychological support), stopping smoking if he smokes, a Mediterranean-style diet, weight management and moderating alcohol. He also needs advice on returning to manual work and on DVLA driving rules.

questions.q: "In heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, the drugs that make patients feel better are not always the drugs that make them live longer." Discuss this statement. Your answer should explain the neurohormonal model of chronic heart failure and use it to compare the mechanisms and roles of loop diuretics, digoxin, ACE inhibitors (or ARBs/sacubitril-valsartan), beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists and SGLT2 inhibitors. Conclude by evaluating the strengths and limitations of the neurohormonal model.
markScheme: Neurohormonal model: reduced cardiac output activates the sympathetic nervous system, RAAS and ADH; initially compensatory (maintains BP and perfusion) but sustained activation causes vasoconstriction, salt and water retention, myocyte toxicity, fibrosis and adverse remodelling: a vicious cycle.
Natriuretic peptides are the counter-regulatory system (natriuresis, vasodilation), but their effect is overwhelmed.
Loop diuretics: block NKCC2, reduce congestion and preload, rapidly relieving breathlessness and oedema; not shown to improve survival; can further activate RAAS; electrolyte and renal effects.
Digoxin: Na+/K+-ATPase inhibition increases contractility and vagal tone; the DIG trial (1997) showed reduced hospitalisation but no effect on mortality; narrow therapeutic index.
ACE inhibitors/ARBs/sacubitril-valsartan: block angiotensin II effects (vasoconstriction, aldosterone, remodelling); ARNI also boosts natriuretic peptides; reduce mortality and hospitalisation.

Beta-blockers: block chronic sympathetic toxicity, slow HR, reduce arrhythmias, reverse remodelling; reduce mortality but may worsen symptoms transiently at initiation: a clear example of the statement.
MRAs: block aldosterone-mediated sodium retention and myocardial fibrosis ('aldosterone escape' despite ACEi); reduce mortality; risk hyperkalaemia.

SGLT2 inhibitors: reduce heart failure hospitalisation and cardiovascular death in HFrEF; mechanisms incompletely understood (natriuresis/osmotic diuresis, metabolic and haemodynamic effects), showing benefit beyond the classic neurohormonal model.

Evaluation: model explains why disease-modifying drugs block neurohormones and why inotropes/symptom drugs did not improve survival; limitations: does not explain SGLT2 benefit fully, HFpEF has shown at most modest benefit from neurohormonal blockade (e.g. MRAs), whereas SGLT2 inhibitors do reduce HF events there, individual variation, adverse effects limit titration; the statement is broadly true but some drugs both relieve symptoms and prolong life (e.g. ACEi improve symptoms over time).
Coherent essay structure with a reasoned conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
The statement captures a key lesson of heart failure pharmacology. In HFrEF a fall in cardiac output is sensed as underfilling of the arterial circulation. The sympathetic nervous system, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) and ADH are activated. In the short term these responses keep blood pressure and organ perfusion up. When sustained, they cause vasoconstriction (raising afterload), salt and water retention (causing congestion), direct myocyte toxicity, fibrosis and progressive ventricular remodelling, a vicious cycle that drives the disease forward. Natriuretic peptides oppose these effects but are overwhelmed.

Loop diuretics such as furosemide block NKCC2 in the loop of Henle. They remove excess fluid and lower filling pressures, so breathlessness and oedema improve quickly. They have not been shown to prolong life, and the fall in volume can further activate the RAAS. Digoxin raises contractility by inhibiting the Na+/K+-ATPase and increases vagal tone. In the DIG trial (1997) it reduced hospital admissions but had no effect on mortality. Both drugs are mainly for symptoms.

The drugs that improve survival block the neurohormonal cycle. ACE inhibitors and ARBs reduce the effects of angiotensin II. Sacubitril-valsartan also blocks neprilysin, enhancing the natriuretic peptides, and is superior to an ACE inhibitor in eligible patients. Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists block aldosterone, which 'escapes' ACE inhibition, reducing sodium retention and myocardial fibrosis; hyperkalaemia limits their use. Beta-blockers best illustrate the statement. Acutely they reduce contractility and may make patients briefly feel worse, yet over months they slow the heart, reduce arrhythmias, reverse remodelling and substantially lower mortality. That is why they are started low and increased gradually.

SGLT2 inhibitors complicate the story. Dapagliflozin and empagliflozin reduce heart failure hospitalisation and cardiovascular death, but their benefit is not fully explained by neurohormonal blockade; natriuresis and metabolic and haemodynamic effects have been proposed.

The neurohormonal model has been very successful. It explained why positive inotropes and vasodilators did not improve survival and predicted the benefit of RAAS and sympathetic blockade. But it does not fully explain the SGLT2 inhibitors, and it has worked much less well in HFpEF, where similar drugs have shown limited benefit. In conclusion, the statement is broadly true, but the line is blurred: disease-modifying drugs also improve symptoms and reduce hospitalisation over time, while diuretics remain essential for quality of life.

questions.q: The sensitivity of a diagnostic test is best defined as:
options: The proportion of people with a positive test who have the disease
The proportion of people without the disease who test negative
The proportion of people with the disease who test positive
The proportion of all test results that are correct
questions.why: Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN). 'Proportion of positives who have the disease' is PPV, and 'proportion of disease-free who test negative' is specificity.

questions.q: A 78-year-old man with atrial fibrillation has treated hypertension and had a transient ischaemic attack last year. He has no other conditions. What is his CHA2DS2-VASc score?
questions.why: Age 75 or over scores 2, hypertension 1, and previous stroke/TIA 2, giving 5; male sex scores 0.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman has pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness 10 days after knee surgery. Her two-level Wells score for PE is 6. Following NICE guidance, what is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?
options: Measure D-dimer and only image if it is raised
Arrange CT pulmonary angiography (with interim anticoagulation if it is delayed)
Discharge with advice because a normal ECG excludes PE
Request a lower limb Doppler ultrasound only
questions.why: With a Wells score over 4, PE is 'likely', so imaging with CTPA is needed directly; a negative D-dimer cannot safely rule out PE at this pre-test probability.

questions.q: State what each letter of the ABCDE approach stands for and give two principles of how it is used in an acutely unwell patient.
markScheme: Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure (all five needed for the mark).
Problems are treated as they are found, in order, before moving to the next step (life-threatening problems first).
Reassess after every intervention and if the patient deteriorates; call for help early (e.g. using SBAR).
questions.modelAnswer: ABCDE stands for Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability (neurological status, including conscious level and glucose) and Exposure (full examination, temperature, looking for rashes, bleeding or other clues). It orders assessment by what kills fastest: an obstructed airway kills sooner than a breathing problem, which kills sooner than circulatory failure. Each problem is treated as soon as it is found, before moving on. The patient is reassessed from the top after every intervention and whenever they deteriorate, and help is called early, with handover structured using a tool such as SBAR.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by 'anchoring bias' and 'premature closure' in clinical reasoning, illustrating each with an example from cardiorespiratory medicine, and suggest two strategies to reduce them.
markScheme: Anchoring: fixing on an early impression or salient feature and failing to adjust when new information appears.
Example: labelling breathlessness in a known asthmatic as 'just asthma' and missing a pulmonary embolism; or calling chest pain musculoskeletal after an early normal ECG.

Premature closure: accepting a diagnosis before it has been verified, so the search stops once a plausible explanation is found (e.g. stopping at 'chest infection' in a patient whose raised JVP and S3 point to heart failure).

Strategies: deliberately generate a differential and ask 'what else could this be?' and 'what must not be missed?'; use checklists/structured approaches; seek a second opinion; use diagnostic time-outs and safety-netting; reflect on cases.
questions.modelAnswer: Anchoring bias is fixing on an early impression or a striking feature and failing to adjust it as new information arrives. For example, breathlessness in a known asthmatic may be assumed to be an exacerbation, missing a pulmonary embolism suggested by tachycardia, normal peak flow and a recent long-haul flight. Premature closure is accepting a diagnosis before it has been confirmed and stopping the search once a plausible explanation has been found, for instance diagnosing a chest infection and ignoring a raised JVP and third heart sound pointing to heart failure. Useful strategies are routinely asking 'what else could this be, and what must I not miss?', using structured approaches and checklists, diagnostic time-outs, and senior or peer review.

questions.q: In a 5-year trial, a new lipid-lowering drug reduced the rate of major cardiovascular events from 10% in the placebo group to 7.5% in the treatment group. Calculate the absolute risk reduction, relative risk reduction and number needed to treat, and explain why the same relative risk reduction would give a different NNT in a low-risk population.
markScheme: NNT = 1 / 0.025 = 40 people treated for 5 years to prevent one event.

If baseline risk were lower (e.g. 2%), the same 25% RRR gives an ARR of only 0.5% and an NNT of 200, so benefit depends on baseline risk; this is why treatment decisions use absolute risk (e.g. QRISK3).
questions.modelAnswer: The absolute risk reduction is the difference in event rates: 10% - 7.5% = 2.5% over 5 years. The relative risk reduction is that difference divided by the control rate: 2.5/10 = 25%. The number needed to treat is 1/ARR = 1/0.025 = 40, so 40 people must take the drug for 5 years to prevent one major event. Relative reductions are fairly constant, but absolute benefit depends on baseline risk. In a group with only a 2% five-year risk, a 25% relative reduction gives an ARR of 0.5% and an NNT of 200. This is why decisions such as statin prescribing are based on absolute risk scores like QRISK3.

questions.q:
Doris, a 74-year-old widow, is brought in by her daughter with 3 days of productive cough and fever. Today she is muddled about the date and where she is, which is new. Observations: respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 91% on room air, blood pressure 98/58 mmHg, heart rate 112/min, temperature 38.6 C. Bloods: urea 9.2 mmol/L, raised CRP and white cell count. Chest X-ray: right lower lobe consolidation.

Using the scoring systems below, explain your reasoning in full.
NEWS2 bands (scale 1): RR 21-24 = 2, 25 or more = 3; SpO2 92-93% = 2, 91% or less = 3; on air = 0; systolic BP 91-100 = 2; pulse 111-130 = 2; new confusion = 3; temperature 38.1-39.0 = 1.

(a) Calculate her NEWS2 score and state what response it should trigger. (b) Calculate her CURB-65 score and explain what it indicates. (c) Explain the physiological basis of her hypoxaemia, tachycardia and hypotension. (d) Discuss the strengths and limitations of using such scores in clinical decision-making.
markScheme: NEWS2: RR 3 + SpO2 3 + air 0 + SBP 2 + pulse 2 + new confusion 3 + temperature 1 = 14.
A score of 7 or more triggers an emergency response: immediate assessment by a clinician with critical care competencies, continuous monitoring, consider higher level of care.
CURB-65: Confusion 1, Urea over 7 mmol/L 1, RR 30 or more 0 (26), BP (systolic below 90 or diastolic 60 or less) 1, age 65 or over 1 = 4.
CURB-65 of 3-5 = high severity with substantial predicted 30-day mortality: hospital management, consider critical care review (especially 4-5).
Hypoxaemia: alveoli filled with exudate are perfused but not ventilated, producing shunt/low V/Q; hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction only partly compensates.

Tachycardia and hypotension: sepsis causes cytokine-mediated vasodilation and capillary leak (reduced SVR and effective volume); fever and dehydration add; tachycardia is baroreflex and sympathetic compensation; raised urea reflects dehydration/reduced renal perfusion.
Strengths: objective, reproducible, prompt escalation, common language, validated against outcomes.

Limitations: scores support but do not replace judgement; may under-score patients on beta-blockers, the elderly (blunted responses) or with chronic hypoxia (scale 2 needed); do not account for frailty, comorbidity or patient wishes; derived in specific populations.
Relates scores to actions: oxygen to target, cultures, antibiotics within the sepsis time frame, fluids, senior review; clear structure.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) NEWS2: respiratory rate 26 scores 3, SpO2 91% scores 3, room air 0, systolic 98 scores 2, pulse 112 scores 2, new confusion 3 and temperature 38.6 scores 1, giving a total of 14. A score of 7 or more needs an emergency response: immediate review by a clinician with critical care skills, continuous monitoring and consideration of transfer to a higher level of care.

(b) CURB-65: new confusion 1; urea above 7 mmol/L 1; respiratory rate below 30 so 0; diastolic 58 (60 or less) 1; age 65 or over 1, giving 4. Scores of 3-5 indicate high-severity pneumonia with a substantial 30-day mortality, needing hospital care and, at 4-5, assessment for critical care.

(c) In consolidated lung, alveoli are full of inflammatory exudate but are still perfused. Blood passing through them is not oxygenated (shunt and low V/Q regions), and mixing it with oxygenated blood lowers arterial PO2. Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction diverts some blood away, but in lobar consolidation this is incomplete. Her low blood pressure reflects sepsis: inflammatory mediators dilate vessels and make capillaries leaky, so systemic vascular resistance and effective circulating volume fall. Fever, poor intake and losses make her dehydrated, which the raised urea also suggests. Tachycardia reflects baroreflex and sympathetic compensation, plus fever. Confusion reflects reduced cerebral perfusion, hypoxaemia and systemic inflammation.

These findings should lead to controlled oxygen to target, blood cultures and prompt antibiotics, careful fluids, monitoring of urine output and early senior review.

(d) Scores are objective, reproducible and quick. They give staff a common language and prompt escalation, and they have been validated against outcomes. But they support judgement rather than replacing it. Older people and those on beta-blockers may not mount a tachycardia, so they are under-scored. Patients with chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure need SpO2 scale 2. Scores ignore frailty, comorbidity, trends and the patient's own wishes, which are central to deciding on intensive care, and they were derived in particular populations. A low score should never override clinical concern.

questions.q:
Frank, a 61-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension, presents with sudden-onset severe chest pain that began while lifting a heavy box. He describes it as 'tearing' and it radiates through to his back between the shoulder blades. He is sweaty and distressed. Heart rate 108/min; blood pressure 186/104 mmHg in the right arm and 148/86 mmHg in the left arm; SpO2 97% on air. There is a soft early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. The ECG shows sinus tachycardia and left ventricular hypertrophy with no ST elevation. A junior doctor suggests giving antiplatelet and anticoagulant treatment for a 'probable acute coronary syndrome'.

(a) Construct a prioritised differential diagnosis for his chest pain, justifying the most likely diagnosis. (b) Explain the pathophysiology that links his findings to that diagnosis. (c) Explain why antiplatelet and anticoagulant drugs could be dangerous here, and identify the cognitive error involved. (d) Outline the immediate decision-making priorities and the key investigation.
markScheme: Prioritised differential of life-threatening causes: aortic dissection (most likely), acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary embolism, tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, oesophageal rupture; then less urgent causes.
Justification: abrupt tearing pain radiating to the back, onset on exertion/straining, hypertension (major risk factor), inter-arm BP difference over 20 mmHg, new aortic regurgitation murmur.
Pathophysiology: an intimal tear allows blood into the media, creating a false lumen that propagates along the aorta.

Links signs: involvement of the arch/subclavian origin causes pulse and BP differential; root involvement dilates the annulus causing aortic regurgitation (early diastolic murmur); hypertension and medial degeneration predispose.

Complications: extension into coronary ostia (usually right) can cause MI (inferior ST elevation, so a 'STEMI' does not exclude dissection), tamponade from rupture into the pericardium, stroke, limb, mesenteric or renal ischaemia.
Antithrombotics or thrombolysis could promote bleeding from the false lumen, rupture and tamponade, and are potentially fatal.
Cognitive error: anchoring/premature closure ('chest pain = ACS'), availability or framing bias; correct approach is to consider 'must-not-miss' diagnoses.
Priorities: ABCDE, senior help, analgesia, IV access, cross-match blood; blood pressure and heart rate control (e.g. IV beta-blocker) to reduce shear stress, under specialist guidance.
Key investigation: urgent CT aortic angiography (or transoesophageal echo if unstable); type A (ascending) needs emergency cardiothoracic surgery, type B often managed medically.
Well-structured, reasoned answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Life-threatening causes come first: aortic dissection, acute coronary syndrome, pulmonary embolism, tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade and oesophageal rupture. Aortic dissection is most likely. The pain was abrupt, maximal at onset and 'tearing', it radiates to the back, it began during straining, and he has poorly controlled hypertension. The systolic difference between his arms is 38 mmHg, and there is a new early diastolic murmur suggesting aortic regurgitation. ACS remains possible, but none of these features suggests it, and the ECG shows no ST elevation.

(b) A tear in the intima lets blood under pressure into the media, splitting it and creating a false lumen that can extend along the aorta. Chronic hypertension and degeneration of the medial layer are the main predisposing factors. If the flap extends into the arch, it can narrow the subclavian origin, giving unequal arm pressures. Involvement of the aortic root dilates the valve ring, causing aortic regurgitation. The dissection can also occlude the coronary ostia (usually the right), producing an inferior MI that may be mistaken for a primary ACS. It can rupture into the pericardium causing tamponade, or compromise carotid, spinal, mesenteric, renal or limb arteries.

(c) Antiplatelets, anticoagulants or thrombolysis would impair haemostasis in a torn aorta, risking extension, rupture, tamponade and death. The suggestion shows anchoring and premature closure: treating 'chest pain plus risk factors' as ACS and not testing that against the features that do not fit. A deliberate 'what must I not miss?' step would have flagged dissection.

(d) Assess using ABCDE and call senior and specialist help immediately. Give analgesia, establish large-bore IV access and cross-match blood. Heart rate and blood pressure should be lowered carefully, typically starting with an intravenous beta-blocker under specialist guidance, to reduce shear stress on the aortic wall. Urgent CT aortic angiography is the key test (transoesophageal echocardiography if he is too unstable). Dissection involving the ascending aorta (Stanford type A) needs emergency cardiothoracic surgery, whereas type B dissections are often managed medically.

questions.q:
Margaret, a 76-year-old retired teacher, is found to have atrial fibrillation at a routine check. She has treated hypertension and type 2 diabetes, but no history of stroke, heart failure or vascular disease. Her eGFR is 58 mL/min/1.73 m2 and haemoglobin is normal. She takes no antiplatelet drugs and has never had a significant bleed. She is worried because a friend 'had a terrible bleed on blood thinners' and asks whether she could just take aspirin instead.

(a) Calculate her CHA2DS2-VASc score and explain what it means for her stroke risk. (b) Explain the mechanism by which AF causes stroke, and why aspirin is not an appropriate alternative. (c) Compare warfarin and a DOAC (direct oral anticoagulant) for her, including mechanisms and practical considerations. (d) Explain how you would use bleeding risk assessment and shared decision-making to reach a decision with her.
markScheme: CHA2DS2-VASc: age 75 or over 2, hypertension 1, diabetes 1, female sex 1 = 5 (heart failure, stroke/TIA and vascular disease 0).
Score of 2 or more: NICE recommends offering anticoagulation, accounting for bleeding risk; her annual stroke risk is substantially raised.

Mechanism: loss of coordinated atrial contraction leads to stasis, especially in the left atrial appendage, and endothelial/atrial changes plus hypercoagulability (Virchow's triad) lead to thrombus, which can embolise to cerebral arteries; AF-related strokes are often large and disabling.

Aspirin: antiplatelet only; little or no effective protection against AF-related (fibrin-rich, low-flow) thrombus while still causing bleeding; NICE advises against aspirin monotherapy for stroke prevention in AF.
Warfarin: vitamin K antagonist (factors II, VII, IX, X); needs INR monitoring and has many drug/food interactions; time in therapeutic range affects benefit.

DOACs: direct factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban, edoxaban, rivaroxaban) or thrombin inhibitor (dabigatran); NICE first-line in AF; no routine INR, fewer interactions, lower intracranial haemorrhage risk than warfarin; dosing depends on renal function, age and weight; check renal function regularly.

Bleeding risk: use a tool such as ORBIT to identify bleeding risk; address modifiable factors (BP control, avoid NSAIDs/antiplatelets, alcohol, anaemia); a high bleeding score alone is not a reason to withhold anticoagulation.

Shared decision-making: explore her concerns and values, explain absolute risks and benefits in understandable terms (e.g. natural frequencies), discuss alternatives including no treatment, check understanding, document; respects autonomy (Montgomery 2015 standard of material risks).
Mentions also assessing rate control/symptoms and possible echocardiography as part of AF management.
Balanced, well-structured answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) She scores 2 for age 75 or over, 1 for hypertension, 1 for diabetes and 1 for female sex, giving a CHA2DS2-VASc of 5. She has no heart failure, stroke/TIA or vascular disease. Her annual stroke risk is well above the threshold where anticoagulation is beneficial, and NICE recommends offering anticoagulation at 2 or more, taking bleeding risk into account.

(b) In AF the atria quiver rather than contract, so blood stagnates, especially in the left atrial appendage. Atrial endothelial dysfunction and a hypercoagulable state complete Virchow's triad. Fibrin-rich thrombus forms and can embolise to the brain, and these strokes are often large and disabling. Aspirin only inhibits platelets. It gives little or no meaningful protection against this low-flow, fibrin-rich thrombus yet still causes bleeding, so NICE advises against aspirin alone for stroke prevention in AF.

(c) Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, reducing functional factors II, VII, IX and X. It needs regular INR checks, interacts with many drugs and foods, and protects well only when the INR is kept in range. DOACs act directly: apixaban, edoxaban and rivaroxaban inhibit factor Xa, and dabigatran inhibits thrombin. NICE recommends a DOAC first-line in AF. DOACs need no routine INR monitoring, have fewer interactions and cause fewer intracranial haemorrhages than warfarin. Because of her age and reduced eGFR, the choice and dose of DOAC must take renal function into account, which needs regular checking.

(d) A bleeding risk tool such as ORBIT, which NICE recommends, helps identify her risk and modifiable factors: controlling blood pressure, avoiding NSAIDs and antiplatelets, moderating alcohol and treating anaemia. A bleeding score on its own is not a reason to withhold anticoagulation. I would explore what happened to her friend and what matters most to her. Then I would explain, in absolute terms and natural frequencies, how many strokes anticoagulation would prevent and how many serious bleeds it might cause, including the option of no treatment. I would check her understanding and give her time to decide. This follows the Montgomery (2015) standard of disclosing material risks and respects her autonomy. Rate control, symptom review and echocardiography are also part of her AF assessment.

questions.q:
A hospital emergency department uses a D-dimer assay with a sensitivity of 95% and a specificity of 50% for venous thromboembolism.

(a) In a group of 1,000 patients in whom the clinical probability of PE is 10%, construct a 2 x 2 table and calculate the positive and negative predictive values. (b) Repeat the calculation for 1,000 patients in whom the probability of PE is 40%. (c) Calculate the positive and negative likelihood ratios of the test and explain how they relate pre-test to post-test probability. (d) Using your results, explain why NICE guidance uses D-dimer only to rule out PE in patients whose Wells score makes PE 'unlikely', and why D-dimer testing in a frail 85-year-old inpatient with cancer is of limited value. (e) Evaluate the wider risks of over-testing with highly sensitive but non-specific tests in clinical practice.
markScheme: Prevalence 10%: 100 with PE: TP 95, FN 5; 900 without: TN 450, FP 450.
Prevalence 40%: 400 with PE: TP 380, FN 20; 600 without: TN 300, FP 300; PPV = 380/680 = about 56%; NPV = 300/320 = about 94%.
LR+ = 0.95/0.50 = 1.9 (a positive result barely changes probability); LR- = 0.05/0.50 = 0.1 (a negative result substantially lowers probability).
Bayes: post-test odds = pre-test odds x LR; e.g. at 10% pre-test (odds 1:9), a negative result gives odds of about 0.011, i.e. post-test probability about 1.1%.

Interpretation: at low pre-test probability a negative D-dimer reduces probability to an acceptably low level, so PE can be ruled out; at higher probability (e.g. 40%) about 6% of those testing negative still have PE (NPV 94%), which is unsafe, so they go straight to imaging.

Specificity falls in older people, inpatients, cancer, pregnancy, infection and after surgery, so most such patients test positive; the test then adds little information and simply leads to imaging (some use age-adjusted thresholds).

Over-testing: false positives cause further imaging (radiation, contrast nephropathy, cost), incidental findings, overdiagnosis (e.g. small subsegmental PE) and anticoagulation-related bleeding; delays and anxiety; resource use.
Advocates rational testing: estimate pre-test probability first, use clinical prediction rules (Wells, PERC), test only when the result would change management.
Accurate calculations presented clearly with a reasoned conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Among 1,000 patients with a 10% probability, 100 have PE. With 95% sensitivity, 95 test positive (TP) and 5 test negative (FN). Of the 900 without PE, 50% specificity means 450 test negative (TN) and 450 test positive (FP). PPV = 95/(95 + 450) = 95/545, about 17%. NPV = 450/(450 + 5) = 450/455, about 98.9%.

(b) At 40% probability, 400 have PE: 380 TP and 20 FN. Of the 600 without, 300 are TN and 300 FP. PPV = 380/680, about 56%. NPV = 300/320, about 94%.

(c) LR+ = sensitivity/(1 - specificity) = 0.95/0.50 = 1.9. LR- = (1 - sensitivity)/specificity = 0.05/0.50 = 0.1. Post-test odds equal pre-test odds multiplied by the likelihood ratio. At 10% (odds 1:9, about 0.11), a negative test gives odds of about 0.011, roughly a 1.1% probability. A positive test raises the odds only to about 0.21, roughly 17%. Unlike predictive values, likelihood ratios do not depend on prevalence.

(d) In 'unlikely' patients a negative D-dimer brings the probability of PE down to around 1%, low enough to stop investigating and avoid imaging.
