At higher pre-test probability, about 6% of those with a negative result in our example would still have PE, which is too many to miss. So NICE sends patients with a 'likely' Wells score straight to CTPA, and a positive D-dimer in any group only means imaging is needed. Specificity falls further with age, cancer, recent surgery, infection, pregnancy and hospital admission. In a frail 85-year-old inpatient with cancer the D-dimer is almost always raised, so it adds little and simply leads to imaging; age-adjusted thresholds are sometimes used to partly offset this.

(e) Using sensitive but non-specific tests without first judging pre-test probability creates large numbers of false positives. These lead to radiation and contrast exposure, incidental findings, overdiagnosis of small, possibly unimportant emboli, and anticoagulation with its bleeding risk, as well as anxiety, delay and cost. The answer is not to avoid sensitive tests but to use them rationally: estimate probability first using structured rules (Wells, and PERC in very low-risk patients), and test only when the result would change management.

questions.q:
Amina, a 29-year-old woman who moved to the UK from a country where rheumatic fever is common, is 28 weeks pregnant. She reports increasing breathlessness on exertion, two episodes of waking at night breathless and palpitations. She recalls being treated for 'joint pains and fever' as a child. Pulse 118/min, irregularly irregular; BP 112/70 mmHg. On auscultation there is a loud first heart sound, an opening snap and a low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble at the apex, best heard with the bell with her lying on her left side. Fine crackles are heard at both lung bases.

(a) Identify the most likely valve lesion and its cause, explaining the pathogenesis from the childhood illness. (b) Explain how the lesion produces each auscultatory finding. (c) Explain why her symptoms have worsened during pregnancy. (d) Explain how the lesion has led to atrial fibrillation and pulmonary congestion, and why AF in this setting carries a particularly high stroke risk.
markScheme: Mitral stenosis due to rheumatic heart disease.

Pathogenesis: group A streptococcal pharyngitis triggers antibodies/T cells that cross-react with cardiac antigens (molecular mimicry), causing acute rheumatic fever with pancarditis; repeated attacks cause valve inflammation, then fibrosis, commissural fusion, leaflet thickening/calcification and chordal shortening over years.
Loud S1: the mitral leaflets are held widely open by the high atrial pressure until ventricular systole, then close forcefully over a wide excursion (while still mobile).

Opening snap: sudden tensing of the stenosed, still-pliable leaflets as they open in early diastole; mid-diastolic rumble: turbulent flow across the narrowed orifice driven by the left atrial-ventricular pressure gradient (presystolic accentuation is lost in AF).
Pregnancy: blood volume and cardiac output rise substantially and heart rate increases; increased flow across a fixed stenosis raises the gradient and left atrial pressure.
Tachycardia shortens diastole disproportionately, reducing filling time across the stenosis and raising LA pressure further.
Raised LA pressure is transmitted to pulmonary veins and capillaries, causing pulmonary oedema (crackles, PND), and over time reactive pulmonary hypertension and right heart strain.
LA pressure overload causes atrial dilatation and fibrosis, the substrate for AF; AF removes atrial contraction and causes a fast rate, causing acute decompensation.

Stroke risk is very high: stasis in a large left atrium plus AF (and pregnancy-related hypercoagulability); rheumatic moderate-severe mitral stenosis with AF is managed with anticoagulation regardless of CHA2DS2-VASc and is a recognised exception to DOAC use in standard guidance (warfarin/heparin choices complicated by pregnancy, specialist management).
Well-structured answer integrating pathology and haemodynamics.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The findings point to mitral stenosis, almost certainly rheumatic. In childhood a group A streptococcal throat infection probably triggered acute rheumatic fever (her 'joint pains and fever'). Antibodies and T cells against streptococcal antigens cross-react with cardiac proteins (molecular mimicry), causing pancarditis. Repeated or severe attacks inflame the valves, which then scar over years. The mitral commissures fuse, the leaflets thicken and may calcify, and the chordae shorten, narrowing the orifice.

(b) In mitral stenosis left atrial pressure stays high throughout diastole, holding the leaflets wide open until ventricular systole. They then close from a wide position, giving a loud S1 while the leaflets remain mobile. In early diastole the stiff but pliable leaflets snap taut as they open, producing the opening snap. Blood then flows turbulently through the narrow orifice under a pressure gradient, giving a low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble at the apex, best heard with the bell in the left lateral position. In sinus rhythm atrial contraction accentuates the rumble before systole; this is lost in AF.

(c) Pregnancy raises blood volume and cardiac output substantially and increases heart rate. The gradient across a fixed stenosis rises steeply with flow, so left atrial pressure rises. Tachycardia shortens diastole more than systole, leaving less time for the left atrium to empty, which raises pressure further. A previously tolerated lesion therefore decompensates, often in the second and third trimesters.

(d) Chronically raised left atrial pressure is transmitted backwards to the pulmonary veins and capillaries. When capillary pressure exceeds plasma oncotic pressure, fluid enters the interstitium and alveoli, causing crackles, exertional breathlessness and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea. Over time reactive pulmonary hypertension and right heart strain may follow. Pressure overload also dilates and scars the left atrium, providing the substrate for AF. AF removes atrial contraction and speeds the ventricular rate, worsening filling and congestion. A large, stagnant left atrium behind a stenotic valve is highly thrombogenic, and pregnancy adds hypercoagulability, so stroke risk is very high. Moderate to severe rheumatic mitral stenosis with AF is treated with anticoagulation regardless of the CHA2DS2-VASc score, and in pregnancy the choice of agent needs specialist cardiology and obstetric management.

questions.q:
Ken, a 64-year-old man, presents with 40 minutes of crushing central chest pain and sweating. Heart rate 46/min, BP 88/54 mmHg, SpO2 96% on air. His chest is clear on auscultation and his JVP is raised. The 12-lead ECG shows 3 mm ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF, ST depression in I and aVL, and a PR interval of 0.28 s with every P wave followed by a QRS.

(a) Interpret the ECG fully, including the conduction abnormality. (b) Identify the most likely culprit coronary artery and explain how its anatomy accounts for his bradycardia. (c) His chest is clear but his JVP is raised and he is hypotensive. Explain what additional complication this suggests, how you could look for it on an ECG, and the physiology behind it. (d) Explain why glyceryl trinitrate could be dangerous in this situation.
markScheme: Sinus bradycardia at 46/min.
Inferior STEMI: ST elevation in contiguous inferior leads II, III, aVF with reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL.
PR 0.28 s (over 0.20 s) with 1:1 conduction = first-degree AV block.
Culprit: most often the right coronary artery (in right-dominant circulation); ST depression in I and aVL favours RCA over circumflex (ST elevation greater in III than II would also favour RCA).

The RCA supplies the SA nodal artery in about 60% and the AV nodal artery in most people (right dominance), so ischaemia slows the sinus rate and AV conduction; inferior ischaemia also increases vagal tone (Bezold-Jarisch reflex).
Clear lungs, raised JVP and hypotension suggest right ventricular infarction (RCA supplies most of the RV).
Look with right-sided chest leads: ST elevation in V4R (also ST elevation in V1 may be seen).

Physiology: an ischaemic RV cannot pump blood through the lungs, so right-sided venous pressure rises (raised JVP) while LV filling and output fall (hypotension) without pulmonary congestion; LV output is highly preload-dependent.

GTN causes venodilation and reduces preload, which can cause profound hypotension in RV infarction (and is avoided if systolic BP is low); bradycardia also limits compensation; treatment prioritises urgent reperfusion (primary PCI) and careful fluid support under senior guidance.
Systematic ECG interpretation and logical structure.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The ECG shows sinus bradycardia at 46/min. There is 3 mm ST elevation in the contiguous inferior leads II, III and aVF with reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL, which is an acute inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction. The PR interval of 0.28 s is prolonged (normal 0.12-0.20 s), but every P wave is conducted, so this is first-degree AV block.

(b) Inferior STEMI is most often caused by occlusion of the right coronary artery in a right-dominant circulation; the reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL favours the RCA over the circumflex (ST elevation greater in III than in II would also point to the RCA). The RCA gives off the SA nodal artery in about 60% of people and, in right-dominant circulations, the AV nodal artery. Ischaemia of these structures slows the sinus rate and delays AV conduction. Inferior wall ischaemia also activates cardiac vagal afferents, increasing parasympathetic tone (the Bezold-Jarisch reflex), which adds to the bradycardia and hypotension. Higher degrees of AV block can develop, so he needs monitoring.

(c) Hypotension with a raised JVP and clear lungs suggests right ventricular infarction, since the RCA supplies most of the right ventricle. The ischaemic right ventricle cannot push enough blood through the lungs. Venous blood backs up, raising the JVP, while left ventricular filling and output fall, causing hypotension without pulmonary oedema. It can be detected with right-sided chest leads, looking for ST elevation in V4R; echocardiography also shows a dilated, hypokinetic right ventricle.

(d) In RV infarction, cardiac output depends on adequate preload to drive blood through the failing right ventricle. GTN is mainly a venodilator, so it reduces venous return and can cause profound hypotension. He is already hypotensive and bradycardic, which is a further reason to avoid it. The priority is urgent reperfusion with primary PCI, with careful haemodynamic support, including cautious fluids, under senior and cardiology guidance.
